source: Phase 41 (2026-10-18): original questions on the chapters of Beast Academy Levels 1-5 and the AoPS books, written by Claude Sonnet from our own chapter summaries (docs/question-bank-beast-academy.md) and solved blind by Claude Opus (Claude Code agents, not runAi: no ai_runs rows), code-checked by lintQuestion; "checked" questions await a platform admin. Algebra 14-22 and Introduction to Geometry added 2026-10-22 by the same pipeline.

notes.GEO.01: Text-only: every figure is described by letters, order, lengths or coordinates. All 69 requested were written; counting skills carry a little over a third because the summary names them and they support many distinct set-ups.
notes.GEO.03: No figures: triangles are described by their sides and angles and the matching corners are stated. Where AAS is the rule, ASA is not offered as a distractor (the two are interchangeable once the third angle is found), and vice versa. Pythagoras, similarity and trigonometry are not used; the triangle inequality is used only in two isosceles-perimeter questions. All 69 requested were written.
notes.GEO.05: All 69 written; no figure needed (every triangle is given by sides, angles and stated vertex correspondence). Skills: AA similarity, corresponding sides and scale factor, perimeters, areas, indirect measurement, a line parallel to a side, and similar triangles inside a figure (altitude to the hypotenuse, shared angle, inscribed square). Irrational answers avoided.
notes.GEO.06: All 69 written; no figure needed (every triangle is given by its side lengths, angles or a described solid). Skills: Pythagorean theorem for a hypotenuse and for a leg, triples and the converse, 45-45-90, 30-60-90, and applications (diagonals, ladders, distances, coordinates, 3D). Irrational answers are choice questions.
notes.GEO.09: Text-only: every figure is described by letters in order, lengths and angle measures. All 69 requested were written. Questions on a hexagon's area that need a radical are choice questions.
notes.GEO.10: Text-only: triangles are described by their side lengths and angles in words; no figure is needed. All 69 requested were written. Where angles and sides are both given, only their ORDER is used, never exact values, so no question describes an impossible triangle.
notes.GEO.11: All 69 written; every figure is described in words (centers, radii, tangent points, named chords). Answers in terms of pi are choice questions or are asked as "k pi, what is k". Skills: radius and diameter, circumference, area, arcs and arc length, sectors, chords, tangent lines (the last includes tangent segments, incircle and circumscribed quadrilateral). Pass A items on the same ideas were not reused.
notes.GEO.12: All 69 written; no figure needed: every arc and angle is named by its points and, where several arcs meet, by the order of the points around the circle. Skills: central angles and arcs, inscribed angles, angle in a semicircle and angles on the same arc, inscribed quadrilaterals, two chords crossing inside, tangent-chord and tangent-radius, and angles outside the circle from two secants or a tangent. All answers are whole degrees, lengths are integers or 7.5. Pass A items on the same ideas were not reused.
notes.GEO.15: Text only. Answers with pi are choice questions or are asked as k in k*pi; the rolled-up half circle and the rolled sheet are described in words only.
notes.GEO.16: No figures are used: every transformation is described in words with the coordinates written out, and every key was recomputed by code (translation, the four reflections, 90-degree and 180-degree rotations about the origin and about another point, and dilations about the origin and about another point). Answers that are coordinate pairs are always choice questions. Rotations are always stated as clockwise or counterclockwise, with the usual axes (x to the right, y up). All 30 requested were written.
notes.GEO.17: All 30 written in full. Equations (lines, circles) are choice questions; distances use Pythagorean triples so numeric answers stay rational. Area of polygons is by rectangles/trapezoids and by cutting off right triangles, with the shoelace formula mentioned only as a check.
notes.GEO.18: No calculator values are used: every question rests on the exact values at 30, 45 and 60 degrees, on side ratios of Pythagorean triples, or on sines and cosines given in the stem. Answers with square roots are choice questions. The one obtuse angle (120 degrees) gives its cosine in the stem. 30 questions, 10 per difficulty.
notes.GEO.02: Text-only geometry: every figure is described in words (which lines are parallel, which side is extended, where a point lies). Angles are never read from a drawing. Parallel lines, triangle angle sums, exterior angles and polygon angle sums are all fully testable in words; no content was left out, but diagrams-heavy "find the angle in this picture" problems were avoided or rewritten as described configurations. 99 written.
notes.GEO.04: No figures are used: every shape is described by its measurements, a list of corner coordinates or a statement of where points lie. Pythagoras is deliberately not needed. All 99 requested were written.
notes.GEO.07: Text-only: every figure is described by its measurements. Answers that would be irrational are avoided or posed as a decimal; several keys use 3-4-5, 5-12-13 and 9-12-15 triangles.
notes.GEO.08: Text-only: every figure is described by lengths, angles and vertex order, with a named labelling (for example AB parallel to CD). Mixed with a few classification questions; no question depends on a picture. Surds appear only in the one wrong option of a choice question.
notes.GEO.13: Text-only: every point and segment is named in the stem and the "A then B" order along a line is stated, so no figure is needed. Answers are whole numbers or one radius; none needs a surd. Where an equation is needed the quadratic factors over the integers. 30 questions, 10 per difficulty.
notes.GEO.14: Text-only: solids are described by their measurements. Pyramids are square or rectangular with the apex above the center; prisms are right prisms. Irrational diagonals are choice questions. Cone, cylinder and sphere work is not part of the summary and is left out.
notes.GEO.19: Text-only: every figure is described by its measurements and the named points, with no picture needed. Answers are whole numbers or terminating decimals (no surds), so square roots appear only inside solutions. 30 questions, 10 per difficulty; skills are spread 6/7/6/6/5.

questions.stem: Which of these figures has exactly one endpoint?
questions.solution: A ray starts at one point, its endpoint, and goes on forever in one direction. A line segment has two endpoints, a line has none, and a polygon is a closed figure with no endpoints.

solve.work: A ray starts at one endpoint and goes on forever in one direction. A line has none, a segment has two, a polygon is closed.

questions.stem: A line segment has 2 endpoints, a ray has 1 endpoint and a line has no endpoints. Mia draws 3 segments, 4 rays and 5 lines. How many endpoints do her figures have in all?
questions.solution: The 3 segments have $3 \times 2 = 6$ endpoints, the 4 rays have $4 \times 1 = 4$, and the lines have none. In all, $6 + 4 + 0 = 10$.

solve.work: Segments: 3 x 2 = 6. Rays: 4 x 1 = 4. Lines: 5 x 0 = 0. Total 6 + 4 + 0 = 10.

questions.stem: A figure is named ray $MN$. Which point is its endpoint?
questions.solution: A ray is named with its endpoint first and then another point on the ray. So the endpoint of ray $MN$ is $M$, and the ray passes through $N$ and goes on past it.

solve.work: A ray is named with its endpoint first, so ray MN starts at M and passes through N.

questions.stem: Angle $XYZ$ is made by two rays that start at the same point. Which point is the vertex of the angle?
questions.solution: The vertex is the point where the two rays meet. In the name of an angle written with three letters, the vertex is the middle letter, so the vertex is $Y$.

solve.work: The middle letter of an angle name is the vertex, so the vertex of angle XYZ is Y.

questions.stem: What is the name of a polygon with 8 sides?
questions.solution: A polygon with 6 sides is a hexagon, with 7 a heptagon, with 8 an octagon and with 9 a nonagon. The polygon with 8 sides is an octagon.

solve.work: An 8-sided polygon is an octagon (6 hexagon, 7 heptagon, 9 nonagon).

questions.stem: In pentagon $ABCDE$, the vertices are listed in order around the figure. Which two vertices are next to vertex $C$?
questions.solution: In the name, each vertex is joined by a side to the letter before it and the letter after it. The letters beside $C$ are $B$ and $D$, so those two vertices are next to $C$.

solve.work: Around the pentagon the order is A-B-C-D-E-A, so C is between B and D.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$ and $C$ are collinear, with $B$ between $A$ and $C$. $AB = 6$ cm and $BC = 9$ cm. How long is $AC$, in centimeters?
questions.solution: Collinear points lie on one line. Since $B$ is between $A$ and $C$, the segment $AC$ is made of $AB$ and $BC$, so $AC = 6 + 9 = 15$ cm.

solve.work: B is between A and C, so AC = AB + BC = 6 + 9 = 15 cm.

questions.stem: Six points are marked on a line. How many different line segments have two of these points as their endpoints?
questions.solution: Each of the 6 points can be paired with 5 others, which is $6 \times 5 = 30$ pairs. Segment $AB$ and segment $BA$ are the same segment, so every segment was counted twice. The answer is $30 \div 2 = 15$.

solve.work: Each pair of the 6 points gives one segment: C(6,2) = 6*5/2 = 15.

questions.stem: Four points are in a plane, and no three of them are on one line. How many different lines pass through two or more of the points?
questions.solution: Each pair of points determines one line, and no line contains three of the points, so different pairs give different lines. There are $\frac{4 \times 3}{2} = 6$ pairs, so there are 6 lines.

solve.work: No three collinear, so each pair gives a different line: C(4,2) = 6.

questions.stem: Five points are in a plane, and no three of them are on one line. How many different triangles can be made with three of the points as vertices?
questions.solution: Any three of the points form a triangle, because no three are collinear. Choosing three points in order gives $5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$ ways, but each triangle is counted $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$ times. So there are $60 \div 6 = 10$ triangles.

solve.work: No three collinear, so every choice of 3 points makes a triangle: C(5,3) = 10.

questions.stem: Which figure goes on forever in both directions?
questions.solution: A line has no endpoints and continues without end in both directions. A segment stops at both ends, and a ray stops at one end only.

solve.work: A line extends without end in both directions; a ray only one way, a segment and an angle are bounded or made of rays.

questions.stem: Which of these has a length that can be measured?
questions.solution: A segment starts and stops at two endpoints, so it has a length. A line and a ray go on forever, and a plane is a flat surface that goes on forever.

solve.work: Only a segment has two endpoints and so a finite measurable length.

questions.stem: Points $J$, $K$, $L$, $M$ and $N$ lie on a line in that order. How many of these five points are on segment $KM$, counting $K$ and $M$ themselves?
questions.solution: Segment $KM$ contains its endpoints $K$ and $M$ and the point $L$ between them. $J$ and $N$ are outside it. That is $3$ points.

solve.work: Segment KM contains K, L, M (J and N lie outside). 3.

questions.stem: Points $R$, $S$ and $T$ lie on a line in that order. Which name is the ray that starts at $T$ and passes through $S$?
questions.solution: A ray is named with its endpoint first. The endpoint is $T$ and the ray passes through $S$, so it is ray $TS$.

solve.work: A ray is named endpoint first, then a point it passes through: ray TS.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on a line in that order. How many of these four points are on ray $BC$?
questions.solution: Ray $BC$ starts at $B$, passes through $C$ and keeps going, so it also passes through $D$. The points on it are $B$, $C$ and $D$, which is $3$ points. $A$ is behind the endpoint.

solve.work: Ray BC starts at B and goes through C and beyond to D: B, C, D. 3.

questions.stem: Which sentence describes ray $ST$ correctly?
choices: It starts at $S$ and stops at $T$
It starts at $S$, passes through $T$ and goes on forever
It starts at $T$, passes through $S$ and goes on forever
It goes on forever in both directions through $S$ and $T$
questions.answer: It starts at $S$, passes through $T$ and goes on forever
questions.solution: The first letter of a ray is its endpoint. Ray $ST$ begins at $S$, goes through $T$ and never stops. Stopping at $T$ would be a segment, and going both ways would be a line.

solve.answer: It starts at $S$, passes through $T$ and goes on forever
solve.work: Ray ST: endpoint S, passes through T and continues forever.

questions.stem: Which is a correct way to write the angle with vertex $Q$ whose sides are ray $QP$ and ray $QR$?
questions.solution: The vertex is the middle letter of an angle name. With vertex $Q$ in the middle and a point on each side at the ends, the name is $\angle PQR$.

solve.work: Vertex letter goes in the middle: angle PQR.

questions.stem: Which of these angles has its vertex at point $T$?
questions.solution: The vertex is the middle letter. In $\angle STU$ the middle letter is $T$. The others have $S$ or $U$ in the middle.

solve.work: Middle letter is the vertex: STU has vertex T; SUT, TUS vertex U; TSU vertex S.

questions.stem: Three rays $BA$, $BC$ and $BD$ start at the same point $B$ and are in that order as you turn from ray $BA$ to ray $BD$, with $\angle ABD$ less than $180^\circ$. How many different angles have two of these three rays as their sides?
questions.solution: The pairs of rays are $BA$ and $BC$, $BC$ and $BD$, and $BA$ and $BD$. That gives $3$ angles.

solve.work: Pairs of rays: (BA,BC), (BC,BD), (BA,BD), all less than 180. 3 angles.

questions.stem: A polygon has 4 vertices. What kind of polygon is it?
questions.solution: A polygon has as many sides as vertices. Four sides make a quadrilateral.

questions.stem: A polygon is named $ABCDEFG$, using seven letters. How many sides does it have?
questions.solution: Each letter is a vertex, and a polygon has as many sides as vertices. So it has $7$ sides.

questions.stem: Pentagon $ABCDE$ has its vertices in order around the figure. Which of these segments is a side of the pentagon?
questions.solution: Sides join vertices that are next to each other in the name. $D$ and $E$ are next to each other. $AC$, $BD$ and $CE$ each skip a vertex, so they cut across the pentagon.

solve.work: Sides are AB, BC, CD, DE, EA. DE is a side; CE, AC, BD are diagonals.

questions.stem: Three points are collinear. Which statement must be true?
choices: They are the corners of a triangle
They are the same distance from each other
Two of them make a right angle with the third
One line passes through all three of them
questions.answer: One line passes through all three of them
questions.solution: Collinear means on one line. So one line passes through all three points. Points on a line cannot be the corners of a triangle.

solve.answer: One line passes through all three of them
solve.work: Collinear means one line passes through all of them.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on a line in that order, with $AB = 3$, $BC = 4$ and $CD = 5$. What is $AD$?
questions.solution: The points are in order along the line, so the lengths add: $AD = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12$.

questions.stem: Which of these sets of three points lie on one line?
questions.solution: The points $(0,1)$, $(2,5)$ and $(4,9)$ each step $2$ across and $4$ up, so they line up. In each of the other sets the steps up are different, so the points do not line up.

questions.stem: Four towns, $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$, are in a row along a straight road. A sign is put up for each pair of towns, giving the distance between them. How many signs are put up?
questions.solution: Each pair of towns is one segment of the road. The pairs are $AB$, $AC$, $AD$, $BC$, $BD$ and $CD$, which is $6$ signs.

questions.stem: A pentagon has 5 vertices. Every two vertices are joined by a segment, the sides and the diagonals together. How many segments are there?
questions.solution: Each vertex joins to the other $4$. That counts every segment twice, so there are $\frac{5 \times 4}{2} = 10$ segments.

questions.stem: Seven fence posts stand in a straight row. A string is stretched between every two posts. How many strings are needed?
questions.solution: Each post is joined to $6$ others, giving $7 \times 6 = 42$ ends, but every string has two ends. So there are $\frac{7 \times 6}{2} = 21$ strings.

questions.stem: Maria marks three dots on paper so that they do not lie on one straight line. She draws a straight line through each pair of dots. How many lines does she draw?
questions.solution: The pairs of dots are $1$ and $2$, $1$ and $3$, and $2$ and $3$. Each pair gives its own line, so she draws $3$ lines.

solve.work: Three non-collinear dots: 3 pairs, 3 distinct lines.

questions.stem: Four points all lie on the same line. How many different lines pass through at least two of the four points?
questions.solution: Any two of the points lie on the one line that holds all four. Every pair gives that same line, so there is only $1$ line.

solve.work: All four on one line: only that line. 1.

questions.stem: Four trees are planted so that no three of them are in a line. Three trees are chosen as the corners of a triangle. How many different triangles can be made?
questions.solution: A triangle is chosen by leaving out one of the four trees. There are $4$ trees to leave out, so $4$ triangles.

questions.stem: Which of these sets of three points are the corners of a triangle?
questions.solution: Three points make a triangle only when they are not on one line. The points $(1,2)$, $(2,4)$, $(3,6)$ lie on a line, as do the points in a row at height $5$ and the points in a column at $x = 3$. The points $(0,0)$, $(2,1)$, $(4,3)$ do not.

solve.work: (0,0),(2,1),(4,3): slopes 1/2 and 1, not collinear. The others lie on x=3, y=2x, y=5.

questions.stem: Points $A$ and $B$ are marked, and four other points $C$, $D$, $E$ and $F$ are marked, with no three of the six points on one line. How many triangles have both $A$ and $B$ as corners?
questions.solution: The third corner can be any of the four other points, and each choice gives a different triangle. So there are $4$ triangles.

solve.work: Third corner is one of C, D, E, F: 4.

questions.stem: Points $P$, $Q$, $R$ and $S$ lie on a line in that order. Which of these names the same figure as line $PQ$?
questions.solution: A line can be named by any two points on it, and $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ are all on one line, so line $RS$ is line $PQ$. A segment has two endpoints and a ray has one, so segment $PQ$, ray $PQ$ and segment $PS$ are all only parts of the line.

solve.work: P, Q, R, S are on one line, so line PQ and line RS are the same line. Segments and the ray are only parts of it.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on a line in that order. Which of these is the same ray as ray $BC$?
questions.solution: Ray $BC$ starts at $B$ and goes through $C$ toward $D$. Ray $BD$ also starts at $B$ and goes the same way, so it is the same ray. Ray $CB$ and ray $CD$ start at $C$, and ray $BA$ goes the other way.

solve.work: Ray BC starts at B and goes through C and on to D. Ray BD starts at B and goes through D (passing C): the same ray. Ray BA goes the other way; rays CD and CB start at C.

questions.stem: Point $D$ is on ray $BA$ and point $E$ is on ray $BC$, and neither is the point $B$. Which of these is another name for $\angle ABC$?
questions.solution: Angle $ABC$ is formed by rays $BA$ and $BC$. Ray $BD$ is the same ray as $BA$ and ray $BE$ is the same as $BC$, so the angle is also $\angle DBE$ or $\angle EBD$. The other names have vertex $D$ or $E$, so they are different angles.

solve.work: Ray BD is ray BA and ray BE is ray BC, so angle ABC = angle DBE = angle EBD (vertex B in the middle). The other options have vertex D or E.

questions.stem: Four rays $BA$, $BC$, $BD$ and $BE$ start at the same point $B$. They are in that order as you turn from ray $BA$ to ray $BE$, and $\angle ABE$ is less than $180^\circ$. How many different angles, each less than $180^\circ$, have two of these four rays as sides?
questions.solution: Every pair of the four rays forms one angle that is less than $180^\circ$. The number of pairs is $\frac{4 \times 3}{2} = 6$.

solve.work: Four rays all within an angle less than 180 degrees; every pair forms an angle less than 180: C(4,2) = 6 (ABC, ABD, ABE, CBD, CBE, DBE).

questions.stem: Quadrilateral $ABCD$ has its vertices in order around the figure. Which of these is NOT a correct name for it?
questions.solution: A correct name lists the vertices in order around the figure, so each letter must be next to the one before it. In $ACBD$, $A$ and $C$ are opposite corners, not neighbors. The other three names start at a different vertex or go the other way around.

solve.work: Valid names follow the cycle A-B-C-D in either direction from any start: ABCD, BCDA, CDAB, DABC, DCBA, CBAD, BADC, ADCB. ACBD uses A-C, a diagonal, so it is not a correct name.

questions.stem: Which of these points is on the same line as $(1, 2)$ and $(3, 6)$?
questions.solution: Going from $(1, 2)$ to $(3, 6)$, $x$ goes up by 2 and $y$ by 4, so $y$ is always twice $x$ along this line. Only $(5, 10)$ has $y$ equal to $2x$.

solve.work: The line through (1,2) and (3,6) has slope 4/2 = 2 and is y = 2x. (5,10) fits; (4,7), (6,10), (5,9) do not.

questions.stem: Eight points are marked on a circle. A chord is a segment whose endpoints are two of the marked points. How many different chords can be drawn?
questions.solution: Each of the 8 points pairs with 7 others, giving $8 \times 7 = 56$ ordered pairs. Each chord is counted twice, so there are $56 \div 2 = 28$ chords.

solve.work: No three points on a circle are collinear; each pair gives one chord: C(8,2) = 28.

questions.stem: Six points are in a plane. Four of them lie on one line, and no other three are collinear. How many different lines pass through at least two of the six points?
questions.solution: There are $\frac{6 \times 5}{2} = 15$ pairs of points. The 6 pairs among the four collinear points all give the same line, so those 6 pairs make only 1 line. The count is $15 - 6 + 1 = 10$.

solve.work: C(6,2) = 15 pairs. The 4 collinear points give C(4,2) = 6 pairs all on one line, so 15 - 6 + 1 = 10 lines.

questions.stem: Seven points are in a plane. Three of them lie on one line, and no other three are collinear. How many triangles have all three vertices among the seven points?
questions.solution: Choosing any 3 of the 7 points gives $\frac{7 \times 6 \times 5}{6} = 35$ choices. Exactly one of them is the three collinear points, which do not form a triangle. So there are $35 - 1 = 34$ triangles.

solve.work: C(7,3) = 35 triples, minus the 1 collinear triple: 34.

questions.stem: Point $A$ is not on line $l$. Points $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ and $F$ are all on line $l$. How many different triangles have all three vertices among these six points?
questions.solution: Three points on $l$ are collinear and make no triangle, so every triangle must use $A$. The other two vertices are chosen from the 5 points on $l$ in $\frac{5 \times 4}{2} = 10$ ways.

solve.work: B to F are collinear, so a triangle needs A and two of the five: C(5,2) = 10.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$ and $C$ lie on a line in that order. Which statement is true?
choices: Ray $AB$ is the same figure as segment $AB$
questions.solution: Ray $AC$ starts at $A$ and passes through $B$ on its way to $C$, so it contains segment $AB$. A longer figure cannot be part of a shorter one, and a ray never stops, so it cannot be a segment or inside one.

solve.work: Ray AC starts at A through B and C, so it contains segment AB. Others false.

questions.stem: Points $P$, $Q$, $R$ and $S$ lie on a line in that order, with $PR = 14$, $QS = 17$ and $QR = 6$. How long is $PS$?
questions.solution: Adding $PR$ and $QS$ counts $QR$ twice, so $PS = 14 + 17 - 6 = 25$. Check: $PQ = 14 - 6 = 8$, $RS = 17 - 6 = 11$, and $8 + 6 + 11 = 25$.

questions.stem: Which of these CANNOT happen for two different lines in a plane?
choices: They cross and make right angles
questions.solution: Two points are enough to fix a line. If two different lines shared two points they would be the same line. Lines can cross at one point (even at right angles) or be parallel and share none.

solve.work: Two distinct lines meet in at most one point; sharing exactly two points is impossible.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on a line in that order. Which statement is true about ray $CB$ and ray $CD$?
questions.solution: Both rays start at $C$, but ray $CB$ goes toward $A$ and ray $CD$ goes toward $D$, in opposite directions. The only point they have in common is $C$.

solve.work: Ray CB goes from C toward B, A; ray CD from C toward D. Opposite rays share only C.

questions.stem: Ray $CD$ starts at point $C$. Point $D$ is $5$ centimeters from $C$. Point $E$ is also on ray $CD$ and is $9$ centimeters from $C$. How far apart are $D$ and $E$, in centimeters?
questions.solution: $D$ and $E$ are on the same ray from $C$, so the distance between them is the difference: $9 - 5 = 4$ centimeters.

solve.work: D and E on the same ray from C: 9 - 5 = 4.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ and $E$ lie on a line in that order. Which of these rays contains $C$ but does not contain $B$?
questions.solution: Ray $CD$ starts at $C$ and goes toward $D$ and $E$, away from $B$. Ray $CA$ goes through $B$ on its way to $A$. Ray $EC$ passes $D$, then $C$, then $B$. Ray $BC$ has $B$ as its endpoint.

solve.work: Ray CD goes C, D, E and on: contains C, not B. Ray CA and ray EC contain B; ray BC contains B.

questions.stem: A paper fan has 5 spokes that all start at its hinge point $O$ and spread out over less than half a turn. Each pair of spokes forms an angle with vertex $O$. How many different angles are formed?
questions.solution: Each of the $5$ spokes pairs with the other $4$, which counts every pair twice. So there are $\frac{5 \times 4}{2} = 10$ angles.

solve.work: C(5,2)=10 angles, all distinct and under 180 since the spread is under half a turn.

questions.stem: Which statement is true about $\angle ABC$ and $\angle CBA$?
choices: They are different angles, because the letters come in a different order
They are two names for the same angle
They have the same vertex but different sides
questions.answer: They are two names for the same angle
questions.solution: The vertex is the middle letter, and it is $B$ in both. The sides are ray $BA$ and ray $BC$ in both. Reversing the end letters gives another name for the same angle.

solve.answer: They are two names for the same angle
solve.work: Same vertex B, same sides BA and BC: same angle.

questions.stem: Which of these angles has the same vertex as $\angle DEF$?
questions.solution: The vertex of $\angle DEF$ is $E$, the middle letter. Only $\angle GED$ has $E$ in the middle.

solve.work: DEF has vertex E; GED has vertex E. FGE vertex G, DFE vertex F, EDG vertex D.

questions.stem: Hexagon $ABCDEF$ has its vertices in order around the figure. Which pair of vertices are next to each other?
questions.solution: The last vertex in the name connects back to the first one, so $F$ and $A$ are joined by a side. $A$ and $C$, $B$ and $E$, and $C$ and $F$ each have vertices between them.

solve.work: Consecutive vertices ... E,F then back to A: F and A are adjacent.

questions.stem: Which of these does NOT name the triangle with vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$?
questions.solution: A triangle can be named by its three vertices in any order. $\triangle ABD$ uses the vertex $D$, so it is a different triangle.

questions.stem: A quadrilateral, a pentagon and a hexagon are drawn. How many vertices do the three polygons have in all?
questions.solution: A polygon has as many vertices as sides, so the total is $4 + 5 + 6 = 15$.

questions.stem: The points $(0, 0)$, $(2, 3)$ and $(k, 9)$ are collinear. What is $k$?
questions.solution: Going from $(0,0)$ to $(2,3)$, the line moves $2$ across for every $3$ up. To reach a height of $9$ it must go up $3$ groups of $3$, so it has gone across $3 \times 2 = 6$. So $k = 6$.

solve.work: Line through origin and (2,3): y=1.5x. 9=1.5k, k=6.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$ and $C$ have $AB = 6$, $BC = 8$ and $AC = 14$. Which statement is true?
choices: The points are on one line, with $B$ between $A$ and $C$
The points are the corners of a triangle
The points are on one line, with $A$ between $B$ and $C$
The points are on one line, with $C$ between $A$ and $B$
questions.answer: The points are on one line, with $B$ between $A$ and $C$
questions.solution: Since $6 + 8 = 14$, going from $A$ to $B$ and then from $B$ to $C$ uses up exactly the distance from $A$ to $C$. So $B$ lies on the way from $A$ to $C$, and the three points are collinear.

solve.answer: The points are on one line, with $B$ between $A$ and $C$
solve.work: AB + BC = 6 + 8 = 14 = AC, so collinear with B between A and C.

questions.stem: Which statement is always true?
choices: Any three points lie on a common line
Any four points lie on a common line
Any three points are the corners of a triangle
Any two points lie on a common line
questions.answer: Any two points lie on a common line
questions.solution: Two points always determine a line. Three points need not be on one line, and three points on a line do not make a triangle.

solve.answer: Any two points lie on a common line
solve.work: Two points always determine a line; the others fail in general.

questions.stem: Eleven points are marked in a row on a line, each $1$ centimeter from the next. How many different segments with endpoints among the marked points are exactly $3$ centimeters long?
questions.solution: A $3$ centimeter segment starts at one of the points and ends $3$ points later. The first point can be any of the first $11 - 3 = 8$ points, so there are $8$ such segments.

questions.stem: A map has 6 towns, with a straight road between every two of them. A seventh town is built, with a straight road to each of the first six. How many new roads are there?
questions.solution: The new town is joined to each of the $6$ old towns, so $6$ new roads are built. The number $15$ counts the old roads and $21$ counts all roads in the end.

solve.work: The new town gets a road to each of the 6: 6 new roads.

questions.stem: A diagonal of a polygon is a segment joining two vertices that are not next to each other. How many diagonals does a pentagon have?
questions.solution: The $5$ vertices have $\frac{5 \times 4}{2} = 10$ segments between pairs. Of these, $5$ are sides, so $10 - 5 = 5$ are diagonals.

questions.stem: Eight points are drawn on a page so that no three lie on one straight line. A student draws a straight line through every pair of points. How many different lines are drawn?
questions.solution: Each pair gives its own line, because no three points share a line. There are $\frac{8 \times 7}{2} = 28$ pairs, so $28$ lines.

questions.stem: Five points are in a plane. Four of them lie on a line $l$, and the fifth point $P$ is not on $l$. How many different lines pass through at least two of the five points?
questions.solution: Line $l$ is one line. Then $P$ makes a different line with each of the $4$ points on $l$, which is $4$ more lines. In all, $1 + 4 = 5$ lines.

solve.work: Line l, plus P joined to each of the 4 points: 1+4 = 5.

questions.stem: Six trees are planted so that no three are in a line. Three of the trees are chosen as the corners of a triangle. How many different triangles can be made?
questions.solution: There are $6 \times 5 \times 4 = 120$ ways to pick three trees in order, and each triangle is counted $6$ times, so there are $\frac{120}{6} = 20$ triangles.

questions.stem: Four points lie on a straight trail, and a fifth point $P$ is off the line of the trail. How many triangles have all three corners among the five points?
questions.solution: A triangle cannot use three points on the trail. So it uses $P$ and two trail points. Two of the $4$ trail points can be chosen in $\frac{4 \times 3}{2} = 6$ ways.

solve.work: Must use P and two of the four collinear points: C(4,2)=6.

questions.stem: Seven points are in a plane, and no three of them are on one line. Point $P$ is one of the seven. How many triangles with all three corners among the seven points do not have $P$ as a corner?
questions.solution: Leave $P$ out. The corners come from the other $6$ points, in $\frac{6 \times 5 \times 4}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = 20$ ways. No three points are on one line, so each choice of three points is a triangle.

solve.work: Triangles without P use 3 of the other 6 points, no three collinear: C(6,3) = 20.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on a line in that order. A ray is named by its endpoint and one other point on it, and different names for the same ray count once. How many different rays can be named using these four points?
questions.solution: From $A$ and from $D$ only one ray is possible (toward the other points). From $B$ and from $C$ there are two rays each, one in each direction. In all, $1 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 6$ rays.

solve.work: From A: ray AB (toward B,C,D) - 1. From B: toward A, toward C - 2. From C: toward B, toward D - 2. From D: toward C - 1. Total 6.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$ and $C$ lie on a line with $B$ between $A$ and $C$. Points $D$, $E$ and $F$ are on the same side of that line, and rays $BA$, $BD$, $BE$, $BF$, $BC$ come in that order as you turn from ray $BA$ to ray $BC$. How many different angles less than $180^\circ$ with vertex $B$ have two of these five rays as sides?
questions.solution: The five rays make $\frac{5 \times 4}{2} = 10$ pairs. But rays $BA$ and $BC$ are on opposite sides of $B$ and make a straight angle of exactly $180^\circ$, which is not less than $180^\circ$. That leaves $10 - 1 = 9$ angles.

solve.work: C(5,2) = 10 pairs of rays; BA and BC are opposite rays (straight angle, 180), so exclude it: 9.

questions.stem: A hexagon has six vertices. Its name is made by listing all six vertices in order around the figure, starting at any vertex and going either clockwise or counterclockwise. How many different names can the hexagon be given?
questions.solution: There are 6 choices for the first vertex. After that, the list can go around in either of 2 directions. So there are $6 \times 2 = 12$ names.

solve.work: 6 possible starting vertices x 2 directions = 12 names.

questions.stem: Pentagon $ABCDE$ has its vertices in order around the figure. Which of these is also a correct name for it?
questions.solution: The sides of the pentagon are $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DE$ and $EA$. In $DCBAE$, the neighbors $D$-$C$, $C$-$B$, $B$-$A$, $A$-$E$ and $E$-$D$ are all sides. The other names pair $A$ with $D$, $C$ with $E$, or $E$ with $B$, and those are not sides.

solve.work: Edges of ABCDE: AB, BC, CD, DE, EA. DCBAE has D-C, C-B, B-A, A-E, E-D: all edges, so correct. EBCDA uses E-B (diagonal); BCEDA uses C-E; ADCBE uses A-D. Only DCBAE.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$ and $C$ are collinear, with $AB = 5$ and $BC = 8$. Which of these could be the length $AC$?
questions.solution: If $B$ is between $A$ and $C$, then $AC = 5 + 8 = 13$. If $A$ is between $B$ and $C$, then $AC = 8 - 5 = 3$. $C$ cannot be between $A$ and $B$, since $BC$ is longer than $AB$. So $AC$ is 13 or 3, and only 13 is listed.

solve.work: If B is between A and C, AC = 13; if A is between, AC = 8 - 5 = 3; if C is between, AB = AC + CB impossible (5 < 8). So AC is 3 or 13; only 13 is offered.

questions.stem: Some points are marked on a page, and no three of them are on one line. Joining every pair of the points by a segment gives exactly 55 segments. How many points are marked?
questions.solution: With $n$ points there are $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ segments. We need $n(n-1) = 110$. Since $11 \times 10 = 110$, there are 11 points.

questions.stem: Nine points are marked on a circle and every two of them are joined by a segment. Then a tenth point is marked on the circle and joined by a segment to each of the nine. How many segments have been drawn in all?
questions.solution: In the end, every pair of the 10 points is joined once, so there are $\frac{10 \times 9}{2} = 45$ segments. Check: the first nine points give 36 segments and the tenth adds 9, and $36 + 9 = 45$.

questions.stem: Five points are in a plane. Exactly three of them lie on one line, and no other three are collinear. How many different lines pass through at least two of the five points?
questions.solution: All $\frac{5 \times 4}{2} = 10$ pairs of points give a line, but the 3 pairs among the collinear points give the same line. So the lines number $10 - 3 + 1 = 8$.

solve.work: C(5,2) = 10 pairs; the 3 collinear points' C(3,2) = 3 pairs share one line: 10 - 3 + 1 = 8.

questions.stem: Three points lie on a line $l$ and four other points lie on a different line $m$. No point is on both lines, and no other three of the seven points are collinear. How many different lines pass through at least two of the seven points?
questions.solution: Line $l$ and line $m$ are two of the lines. Every other line passes through one point of $l$ and one point of $m$, and there are $3 \times 4 = 12$ such pairs, each giving its own line. In all, $1 + 1 + 12 = 14$ lines.

solve.work: C(7,2) = 21 pairs. The 3 on l give 3 pairs on one line; the 4 on m give 6 pairs on one line. 21 - 3 - 6 + 2 = 14 (lines l, m and the 12 cross lines).

questions.stem: A surveyor marks six posts. Four of the posts are in one straight row, and no other three posts are in a straight line. In how many ways can she choose three posts that are the corners of a triangle?
questions.solution: Any 3 of the 6 posts can be chosen in $\frac{6 \times 5 \times 4}{6} = 20$ ways. The choices that fail are the three-post choices from the four in a row, which are $\frac{4 \times 3 \times 2}{6} = 4$ choices. So $20 - 4 = 16$ choices make a triangle.

solve.work: C(6,3) = 20 triples, minus C(4,3) = 4 collinear triples: 16.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on a line in that order, with $AC = 13$, $BD = 15$ and $AD = 22$. How long is $BC$?
questions.solution: Adding $AC$ and $BD$ counts $BC$ twice and covers every other part once, so $AC + BD = AD + BC$. Then $BC = 13 + 15 - 22 = 6$.

solve.work: AC + BD = AD + BC, so BC = 13 + 15 - 22 = 6.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on a line in that order. Which pair of rays has exactly the points of segment $BC$ in common?
questions.solution: Ray $BC$ starts at $B$ and goes toward $C$ and beyond. Ray $CB$ starts at $C$ and goes toward $B$ and beyond. Only the points from $B$ to $C$ are on both. The other pairs share a whole ray, no points, or the longer segment $AD$.

solve.work: Ray BC (B toward C, D) and ray CB (C toward B, A) overlap exactly in segment BC. AC & DB give segment AD; AB & BC give ray BC; BA & CD disjoint.

questions.stem: Which statement is false?
choices: Every ray is part of exactly one line
Every segment is part of exactly one line
Every segment is part of exactly one ray
Every line contains infinitely many points
questions.answer: Every segment is part of exactly one ray
questions.solution: Segment $AB$ is part of ray $AB$ and also of ray $BA$, so a segment lies in more than one ray. A ray or a segment fixes its line, and every line has infinitely many points.

solve.answer: Every segment is part of exactly one ray
solve.work: A segment lies in infinitely many rays (any ray along it starting at or before an endpoint), so "exactly one ray" is false; the others are true.

questions.stem: Five points are marked on a line. How many different rays have one of the five points as their endpoint and also pass through another of the five points?
questions.solution: The two outer points each give $1$ ray, pointing toward the others. Each of the $3$ inner points gives $2$ rays, one in each direction. That is $2 + 3 \times 2 = 8$ rays.

solve.work: End points give 1 ray each (2), each of the 3 interior points gives 2 rays (6): 8.

questions.stem: Ray $AB$ and ray $AC$ are the same ray. Which statement must be true?
choices: $B$ is between $A$ and $C$, and all three are on one line
$C$ is between $A$ and $B$, and all three are on one line
$A$ is between $B$ and $C$, and all three are on one line
$B$ and $C$ are on the same side of $A$, on one line
questions.answer: $B$ and $C$ are on the same side of $A$, on one line
questions.solution: Two rays with the same endpoint $A$ are the same only if they go in the same direction along one line. Then $B$ and $C$ are on the same side of $A$, but either one may be nearer to $A$, so neither "between" statement has to be true.

solve.answer: $B$ and $C$ are on the same side of $A$, on one line
solve.work: Same ray means B and C are on the same side of A on one line; their order is not determined.

questions.stem: Points $P$ and $R$ are on ray $OA$, with $OR$ three times as long as $OP$ and $PR = 14$ centimeters. Point $Q$ is on the ray opposite to ray $OA$, with $OQ$ one centimeter longer than $OP$. How long is $QR$, in centimeters?
questions.solution: $OR - OP = 2 \times OP = 14$, so $OP = 7$ and $OR = 21$. Then $OQ = 8$. $Q$ and $R$ are on opposite sides of $O$, so $QR = 8 + 21 = 29$ centimeters.

solve.work: OP=x, OR=3x, PR=2x=14, x=7, OR=21. OQ=8 on the opposite side: QR=8+21=29.

questions.stem: Six rays $OA$, $OB$, $OC$, $OD$, $OE$ and $OF$ start at the same point $O$, in that order as you turn from $OA$ to $OF$, with $\angle AOF$ less than $180^\circ$. How many angles formed by two of these rays have ray $OC$ strictly inside them, between their sides?
questions.solution: An angle has $OC$ inside it when one side is before $OC$ and the other is after it. There are $2$ rays before $OC$ ($OA$, $OB$) and $3$ after ($OD$, $OE$, $OF$), so $2 \times 3 = 6$ angles.

solve.work: One side from {OA,OB}, the other from {OD,OE,OF}: 2*3 = 6.

questions.stem: Which statement is true about $\angle ABC$ and $\angle CAB$?
choices: They are two names for the same angle
They are different angles that both have vertex $B$
They are different angles, with vertices $B$ and $A$
They are different angles that both have vertex $C$
questions.answer: They are different angles, with vertices $B$ and $A$
questions.solution: The vertex is the middle letter. $\angle ABC$ has vertex $B$, but $\angle CAB$ has vertex $A$, so they are different angles.

solve.answer: They are different angles, with vertices $B$ and $A$
solve.work: ABC has vertex B, CAB has vertex A: different angles.

questions.stem: Point $D$ is on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$, between $B$ and $C$, and segment $AD$ is drawn. How many different angles, each less than $180^\circ$, are formed by pairs of the drawn segments, with vertex $A$, $B$, $C$ or $D$? Count $\angle ABC$ and $\angle ABD$ as the same angle, since they have the same sides.
questions.solution: At $A$ the rays $AB$, $AD$ and $AC$ give $3$ angles. At $B$ there is $1$ angle and at $C$ there is $1$. At $D$ the rays $DA$, $DB$ and $DC$ give $\angle ADB$ and $\angle ADC$, while $\angle BDC$ is a straight angle of $180^\circ$ and is not counted. In all, $3 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 7$.

solve.work: At A: BAD, DAC, BAC (3). At B: ABC (1). At C: ACB (1). At D: ADB, ADC (2; BDC is straight). Total 7.

questions.stem: Octagon $ABCDEFGH$ has its vertices in order around the figure. The diagonal $AE$ cuts it into two polygons. What are they?
questions.solution: One piece has vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, which is $5$. The other has $A$, $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$, which is also $5$. So both pieces are pentagons.

solve.work: Diagonal AE splits into ABCDE and AEFGH: two pentagons.

questions.stem: From one vertex of a polygon, 6 diagonals can be drawn. A diagonal joins two vertices that are not next to each other. How many sides does the polygon have?
questions.solution: From a vertex, no diagonal goes to itself or to its two neighbors. So the polygon has $6 + 3 = 9$ vertices, and $9$ sides.

solve.work: From one vertex n-3 diagonals: n-3=6, n=9.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$ and $C$ lie on a line $l$. Points $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on a line $m$, and $B$ and $C$ are different points. Which statement must be true?
choices: All four points lie on one line
The four points are the corners of a quadrilateral
questions.answer: All four points lie on one line
questions.solution: Two different points $B$ and $C$ are on only one line, so $l$ and $m$ are the same line. Then $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ are all on it.

solve.answer: All four points lie on one line
solve.work: B and C are distinct, so only one line passes through both: l = m, all four on one line.

questions.stem: The points $A(0, 1)$, $B(3, 7)$ and $C(k, k + 10)$ are collinear. What is $k$?
questions.solution: From $A$ to $B$ the line goes up $6$ for every $3$ across, so each step across of $1$ goes up $2$. Its rule is $y = 2x + 1$. For $C$, $k + 10 = 2k + 1$, so $k = 9$. Check: $C = (9, 19)$ and $2 \times 9 + 1 = 19$.

solve.work: Slope AB = 6/3 = 2, line y=2x+1. k+10 = 2k+1, k=9.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$ and $C$ are collinear, with $AB = 10$, $BC = 4$ and $AC = 6$. Which point lies between the other two?
questions.solution: The longest distance is $AB = 10$, and $AC + CB = 6 + 4 = 10$. So going from $A$ to $B$ passes through $C$, and $C$ is between $A$ and $B$.

solve.work: AC + CB = 6 + 4 = 10 = AB, so C is between A and B.

questions.stem: Octagon $ABCDEFGH$ has 8 vertices. A diagonal joins two vertices that are not next to each other. How many diagonals does it have?
questions.solution: All pairs of the $8$ vertices give $\frac{8 \times 7}{2} = 28$ segments. Of these, $8$ are sides, so there are $28 - 8 = 20$ diagonals.

questions.stem: Seven points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$ and $G$ lie on a line in that order. Of all the segments with both endpoints among these points, how many contain the point $D$, counting segments that have $D$ as an endpoint?
questions.solution: A segment contains $D$ when its left end is one of $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ and its right end is one of $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$. That is $4 \times 4 = 16$ choices, but the choice with both ends at $D$ is not a segment. So $15$.

solve.work: Left endpoint from A..D (4), right endpoint from D..G (4), minus D-D: 16 - 1 = 15.

questions.stem: Five points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ and $E$ lie on a line in that order with $AB = BC = CD = DE = 4$ centimeters. How many segments with both endpoints among the five points are at least $8$ centimeters long?
questions.solution: Segments spanning $2$ gaps are $8$ centimeters, and there are $3$ of them. Spanning $3$ gaps there are $2$, and spanning $4$ gaps there is $1$. The total is $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$.

solve.work: 10 pairs, those of length 4 are the 4 adjacent pairs; the other 6 are at least 8.

questions.stem: Lines $l$ and $m$ cross at the point $O$. The marked points are $O$, two other points $A$ and $B$ on $l$, and two other points $C$ and $D$ on $m$. No other three of the five points are on one line. How many different lines pass through at least two of the five marked points?
questions.solution: Line $l$ and line $m$ are two lines. Every other line joins one of $A$, $B$ to one of $C$, $D$, which is $2 \times 2 = 4$ lines. In all, $1 + 1 + 4 = 6$.

solve.work: Line l, line m, plus AC, AD, BC, BD: 6.

questions.stem: Some points are in a plane with no three on one line. A new point is added, again with no three of the points on one line. It makes exactly $9$ new lines. How many points were there before?
questions.solution: The new point makes one new line with each old point, and no other new lines. So the number of new lines equals the number of old points: $9$.

solve.work: New point joins each old point with a new line (no three collinear): n = 9.

questions.stem: Four points are in a plane. Which of these CANNOT be the number of different lines that pass through at least two of the points?
questions.solution: If all $4$ points are collinear there is $1$ line. If $3$ are collinear and one is off the line there are $1 + 3 = 4$ lines. If no three are collinear there are $6$ lines. No arrangement gives $5$.

solve.work: Four points give 1 (all collinear), 4 (exactly three collinear) or 6 (none three). Two collinear triples among 4 points force all 4 collinear, so 5 is impossible.

questions.stem: Four points lie on a line $l$ and three other points lie on a different line $m$. No point is on both lines. Triangles are formed with all three corners among the seven points. How many triangles can be formed?
questions.solution: Pick two corners on $l$ and one on $m$: $6 \times 3 = 18$. Pick one corner on $l$ and two on $m$: $4 \times 3 = 12$. Three corners on one line do not make a triangle. In all, $18 + 12 = 30$.

questions.stem: Points $B$, $D$, $E$ and $C$ lie on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ in that order, and segments $AD$ and $AE$ are drawn. How many triangles are in the figure?
questions.solution: Every triangle has $A$ as a corner and a base made from two of the four points $B$, $D$, $E$, $C$. Two of four points can be chosen in $\frac{4 \times 3}{2} = 6$ ways.

solve.work: Lines from A to B, D, E, C: any two give a triangle: C(4,2) = 6.

questions.stem: Eight points are in a plane. Five of them lie on one line, and no other three are collinear. How many triangles have all three corners among the eight points?
questions.solution: Any $3$ of the $8$ points can be chosen in $\frac{8 \times 7 \times 6}{6} = 56$ ways. The $\frac{5 \times 4 \times 3}{6} = 10$ choices of three from the line are not triangles. So $56 - 10 = 46$.

questions.stem: Two angles are complementary. One measures 35 degrees. How many degrees is the other?
questions.solution: Complementary angles add up to $90^\circ$. So the other angle is $90-35=55$ degrees.

questions.stem: An angle measures 130 degrees. What is the measure of its supplement?
questions.solution: Supplementary angles add up to $180^\circ$. The supplement is $180-130=50$ degrees.

questions.stem: Two straight lines cross. One of the four angles they make measures 72 degrees. How many degrees is the angle directly opposite it (its vertical angle)?
questions.solution: Vertical angles are equal, so the opposite angle is also 72 degrees.

solve.work: Vertical angles are equal, so the opposite angle is 72.

questions.stem: Which pair of angle measures could belong to two supplementary angles?
questions.solution: Supplementary angles add up to $180^\circ$. Only $112+68=180$. The other pairs add up to 190, 90 and 170.

solve.work: Supplementary means sum 180. 112+68 = 180; 45+45 = 90; 112+78 = 190; 100+70 = 170. Only the first.

questions.stem: Two angles sit side by side and together make a straight line. One is 118 degrees. How many degrees is the other?
questions.solution: A straight line is $180^\circ$, so the other angle is $180-118=62$ degrees.

solve.work: Angles on a straight line sum to 180. 180 - 118 = 62.

questions.stem: A line crosses two parallel lines. At the first crossing, one of the angles measures 65 degrees. The corresponding angle at the second crossing measures how many degrees?
questions.solution: When a line crosses two parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal. So the angle is also 65 degrees.

solve.work: Corresponding angles at parallel lines are equal: 65.

questions.stem: A line crosses two parallel lines. Two alternate interior angles are formed, and one of them measures 80 degrees. What does the other measure?
questions.solution: Alternate interior angles between parallel lines are equal, so the other one is also $80^\circ$.

solve.work: Alternate interior angles at parallel lines are equal: 80.

questions.stem: A line crosses two parallel lines. Two co-interior angles (between the parallel lines, on the same side of the crossing line) are formed. One measures 110 degrees. How many degrees is the other?
questions.solution: Co-interior angles between parallel lines add up to $180^\circ$. So the other is $180-110=70$ degrees.

questions.stem: A line crosses two parallel lines. Which statement is true?
choices: Alternate interior angles are always equal
Alternate interior angles always add to $90^\circ$
questions.answer: Alternate interior angles are always equal
questions.solution: Between parallel lines, alternate interior angles are equal and corresponding angles are equal. Co-interior angles add to $180^\circ$ (they are not equal unless both are $90^\circ$).

solve.answer: Alternate interior angles are always equal
solve.work: With parallel lines, alternate interior angles are equal; co-interior angles are supplementary (equal only when 90), corresponding angles are equal (not summing to 180 in general), alternate interior do not sum to 90.

questions.stem: A straight road crosses two parallel train tracks. At the first track, the road makes angles of 70 degrees and 110 degrees with the track (these two angles together make a straight line). At the second track, one angle sits in the same position as the 110 degree angle at the first track (it is its corresponding angle). How many degrees is it?
questions.solution: The two tracks are parallel, so corresponding angles are equal. The angle at the second track is 110 degrees.

solve.work: Corresponding angles at parallel lines are equal, so the corresponding angle of the 110 degree angle is 110.

questions.stem: Two angles of a triangle are 50 degrees and 60 degrees. How many degrees is the third angle?
questions.solution: The angles of a triangle add up to $180^\circ$. The third angle is $180-50-60=70$ degrees.

questions.stem: Which three angle measures could be the angles of a triangle?
questions.solution: The angles of a triangle must add up to $180^\circ$. Only $40+60+80=180$. The other sets add up to 190, 150 and 190.

questions.stem: A right triangle has one angle of 38 degrees besides its right angle. How many degrees is its third angle?
questions.solution: The two acute angles of a right triangle add up to $90^\circ$. So the third angle is $90-38=52$ degrees.

questions.stem: A triangle has two equal angles of 65 degrees each. How many degrees is its third angle?
questions.solution: The three angles add up to $180^\circ$. The third is $180-65-65=50$ degrees.

questions.stem: A triangle has angles of 28 degrees and 62 degrees. What kind of triangle is it?
questions.solution: The third angle is $180-28-62=90$ degrees. A triangle with a $90^\circ$ angle is a right triangle.

solve.work: Third angle = 180 - 28 - 62 = 90, so it is a right triangle.

questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, the interior angles at $B$ and $C$ are 45 degrees and 65 degrees. The exterior angle at $A$ is formed by extending side $BA$ beyond $A$. How many degrees is it?
questions.solution: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles not next to it. So it is $45+65=110$ degrees.

solve.work: Interior A = 180 - 45 - 65 = 70. Exterior angle at A (extending BA past A) = 180 - 70 = 110, which also equals B + C = 45 + 65.

questions.stem: An exterior angle of a triangle measures 120 degrees. One of the two interior angles that are not next to it measures 50 degrees. How many degrees is the other one?
questions.solution: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two far interior angles: $50+?=120$. So the other angle is $120-50=70$ degrees.

solve.work: Exterior angle = sum of the two remote interior angles: 120 = 50 + y, y = 70.

questions.stem: An interior angle of a triangle measures 70 degrees. The exterior angle at the same vertex is made by extending one of its sides. How many degrees does it measure?
questions.solution: The interior and exterior angles at a vertex form a straight line, so they add up to $180^\circ$. The exterior angle is $180-70=110$ degrees.

solve.work: Exterior and interior at the same vertex form a straight line: 180 - 70 = 110.

questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, side $BC$ is extended beyond $C$ to a point $D$. Angle $A$ is 30 degrees and angle $B$ is 80 degrees. How many degrees is angle $ACD$?
questions.solution: Angle $ACD$ is an exterior angle. It equals the two far interior angles added: $30+80=110$ degrees.

solve.work: ACD is the exterior angle at C, equal to A + B = 30 + 80 = 110.

questions.stem: Which statement about an exterior angle of a triangle is true?
choices: It equals the interior angle that is next to it
It equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it
It equals the sum of all three interior angles
It equals the difference of the two interior angles that are not next to it
questions.answer: It equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it
questions.solution: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two far interior angles. It is not equal to the interior angle next to it (those add to $180^\circ$).

solve.answer: It equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it
solve.work: Exterior angle theorem: an exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.

questions.skill: Interior angle sum of a polygon
questions.stem: What is the sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral, in degrees?
questions.solution: A quadrilateral can be split into 2 triangles. Each has an angle sum of $180^\circ$, so the total is $2\times180=360$ degrees.

questions.skill: Interior angle sum of a polygon
questions.stem: What is the sum of the interior angles of a pentagon, in degrees?
questions.solution: A pentagon can be split into 3 triangles, so the sum is $3\times180=540$ degrees.

questions.skill: Interior angle sum of a polygon
questions.stem: What is the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon? Answer in degrees.
questions.solution: A hexagon has 6 sides, so it splits into $6-2=4$ triangles. The sum is $4\times180=720$ degrees.

questions.skill: Interior angle sum of a polygon
questions.stem: Three angles of a quadrilateral measure 85, 95 and 110 degrees. How many degrees is the fourth angle?
questions.solution: The four angles of a quadrilateral add up to $360^\circ$. The three known angles add to 290, so the fourth is $360-290=70$ degrees.

questions.skill: Interior angle sum of a polygon
questions.stem: From one corner of a polygon, diagonals are drawn that split it into 5 triangles. How many sides does the polygon have?
questions.solution: A polygon with $n$ sides splits into $n-2$ triangles. So $n-2=5$ and $n=7$.

solve.work: Diagonals from one vertex split an n-gon into n-2 triangles. n - 2 = 5, n = 7.

questions.stem: How many degrees is each interior angle of a regular hexagon?
questions.solution: The interior angles add up to $(6-2)\times180=720$ degrees. They are all equal, so each is $720\div6=120$ degrees.

questions.stem: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon measures 60 degrees. How many sides does the polygon have?
questions.solution: The exterior angles of any polygon add up to $360^\circ$. With each equal to $60^\circ$, the number of sides is $360\div60=6$.

solve.work: Exterior angles of a polygon sum to 360. 360/60 = 6.

questions.stem: One exterior angle is drawn at each corner of a pentagon. What is the sum of these five exterior angles? Answer in degrees.
questions.solution: The exterior angles of any convex polygon, one at each corner, add up to $360^\circ$, whatever the number of sides.

solve.work: The exterior angles of a convex polygon, one per vertex, sum to 360.

questions.stem: How many degrees is each exterior angle of an equilateral triangle?
questions.solution: Each interior angle is $60^\circ$, and an exterior angle forms a straight line with it. So each exterior angle is $180-60=120$ degrees. (Check: three of them add up to $360^\circ$.)

questions.skill: Angle bisectors and angles around a point
questions.stem: An angle of 80 degrees is cut into two equal angles by its bisector. How many degrees is each of the two angles?
questions.solution: A bisector splits an angle into two equal parts. Each part is $80\div2=40$ degrees.

questions.skill: Angle bisectors and angles around a point
questions.stem: Three angles meet at a point and together fill the whole turn around it. Two of them measure 120 degrees and 150 degrees. How many degrees is the third?
questions.solution: The angles around a point add up to $360^\circ$. The third is $360-120-150=90$ degrees.

solve.work: Angles around a point sum to 360: 360 - 120 - 150 = 90.

questions.skill: Angle bisectors and angles around a point
questions.stem: Ray $OC$ bisects angle $AOB$. Angle $AOC$ measures 27 degrees. What does angle $AOB$ measure?
questions.solution: The bisector splits angle $AOB$ into two equal angles of $27^\circ$. So angle $AOB$ is $2\times27=54$ degrees.

questions.skill: Angle bisectors and angles around a point
questions.stem: Five equal angles fit together around a point and fill the whole turn. How many degrees is each angle?
questions.solution: The angles around a point add up to $360^\circ$. Each of the five angles is $360\div5=72$ degrees.

questions.stem: An angle is 4 times as large as its supplement. How many degrees is the angle?
questions.solution: Let the supplement be $s$. The angle is $4s$, and together they make $180^\circ$: $5s=180$, so $s=36$. The angle is $4\times36=144$ degrees.

questions.stem: Two lines cross, and two of the vertical angles measure $(2x+10)^\circ$ and $(3x-20)^\circ$. What is $x$?
questions.solution: Vertical angles are equal: $2x+10=3x-20$, so $x=30$. Check: both angles are $70^\circ$.

questions.stem: Two angles are supplementary. The larger is 30 degrees more than twice the smaller. How many degrees is the smaller angle?
questions.solution: Let the smaller be $s$. The larger is $2s+30$. Together: $s+2s+30=180$, so $3s=150$ and $s=50$. (The larger is $130^\circ$.)

questions.stem: Angles $P$ and $Q$ are complementary, and $P$ is 18 degrees larger than $Q$. What does angle $P$ measure?
questions.solution: Let $Q=q$. Then $P=q+18$, and $q+q+18=90$, so $q=36$. Angle $P$ is $36+18=54$ degrees.

questions.stem: Two lines cross. One of the four angles measures $3x$ degrees and the angle next to it (together they make a straight line) measures $(2x+20)$ degrees. How many degrees is the smaller of these two angles?
questions.solution: They add up to $180^\circ$: $3x+2x+20=180$, so $x=32$. The angles are $96^\circ$ and $84^\circ$. The smaller is 84 degrees.

questions.stem: A line crosses two parallel lines. A pair of alternate interior angles measure $(3x+15)^\circ$ and $(5x-25)^\circ$. What is $x$?
questions.solution: Alternate interior angles are equal: $3x+15=5x-25$, so $2x=40$ and $x=20$. Each angle is $75^\circ$.

solve.work: Alternate interior angles are equal: 3x + 15 = 5x - 25, 2x = 40, x = 20 (both 75).

questions.stem: A line crosses two parallel lines, and one of the eight angles formed measures 50 degrees. How many of the eight angles measure 50 degrees?
questions.solution: The 50 degree angle has an equal vertical angle at the same crossing, and two more equal angles at the other crossing (a corresponding angle and its vertical angle). That makes 4. The other 4 angles measure $130^\circ$.

solve.work: Of the eight angles, four equal the given angle and four equal its supplement (130), since 50 is not 90. So 4.

questions.stem: A line crosses two parallel lines. Two co-interior angles measure $(x+30)^\circ$ and $(2x)^\circ$. How many degrees is the larger of the two?
questions.solution: Co-interior angles add up to $180^\circ$: $x+30+2x=180$, so $x=50$. The angles are $80^\circ$ and $100^\circ$. The larger is 100 degrees.

solve.work: Co-interior angles are supplementary: x + 30 + 2x = 180, x = 50. Angles 80 and 100. Larger 100.

questions.stem: A line crosses two parallel lines, and one of the eight angles measures $115^\circ$. Which describes all eight angles?
questions.solution: Every angle is either equal to $115^\circ$ or forms a straight line with one, so it is $180-115=65$ degrees. The angles come in equal sets of four: four of $115^\circ$ and four of $65^\circ$.

solve.work: Four angles equal 115 and four equal 180 - 115 = 65.

questions.stem: Line $l$ is parallel to line $m$. A transversal $t$ crosses $l$ at $P$ and $m$ at $Q$. On the right side of $t$, the angle at $P$ below $l$ measures $(3x+10)^\circ$ and the angle at $Q$ above $m$ measures $(2x+20)^\circ$. How many degrees is the angle at $Q$?
questions.solution: Both angles lie between the parallel lines on the same side of $t$, so they are co-interior and add up to $180^\circ$: $5x+30=180$, so $x=30$. The angle at $Q$ is $2(30)+20=80$ degrees.

solve.work: At P below l and at Q above m, both right of t: with l above m these are same-side interior (co-interior) angles; with m above l they are same-side exterior. Either way supplementary: 3x+10 + 2x+20 = 180, x = 30. Angle at Q = 2*30 + 20 = 80 (at P 100).

questions.stem: The angles of a triangle measure $2x$, $3x$ and $4x$ degrees. How many degrees is the smallest angle?
questions.solution: The angles add up to $180^\circ$: $9x=180$, so $x=20$. The smallest angle is $2x=40$ degrees.

questions.stem: The angles of a triangle measure $(2x+5)^\circ$, $(3x)^\circ$ and $(x+25)^\circ$. What is the measure of the largest angle?
questions.solution: The sum is $6x+30=180$, so $x=25$. The angles are $55^\circ$, $75^\circ$ and $50^\circ$. The largest is 75 degrees.

questions.stem: The apex angle of an isosceles triangle is 40 degrees. How many degrees is each base angle?
questions.solution: The two base angles are equal and the three angles add up to $180^\circ$. Each base angle is $(180-40)\div2=70$ degrees.

questions.stem: The two acute angles of a right triangle differ by 20 degrees. How many degrees is the larger one?
questions.solution: The acute angles add up to $90^\circ$. If the smaller is $a$, then $a+a+20=90$, so $a=35$. The larger is 55 degrees.

questions.stem: Which triangle cannot exist?
choices: A triangle with one obtuse angle and two acute angles
A triangle with three acute angles
A triangle with one right angle and two acute angles
A triangle with two obtuse angles
questions.answer: A triangle with two obtuse angles
questions.solution: Two obtuse angles would each be more than $90^\circ$, so they alone would add to more than $180^\circ$. The other triangles all exist.

solve.answer: A triangle with two obtuse angles
solve.work: Two obtuse angles would sum to more than 180, impossible. The others exist.

questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, side $BC$ is extended beyond $C$ to point $D$. Angle $A$ measures $(2x+10)^\circ$, angle $B$ measures $(x+20)^\circ$ and angle $ACD$ measures $(5x-10)^\circ$. How many degrees is angle $ACD$?
questions.solution: The exterior angle equals the two far interior angles: $5x-10=2x+10+x+20$, so $2x=40$ and $x=20$. Angle $ACD=5(20)-10=90$ degrees.

questions.stem: An exterior angle of a triangle measures $130^\circ$. The two interior angles that are not next to it are equal. What does each of them measure?
questions.solution: The exterior angle equals the sum of those two equal angles, so each is $130\div2=65$ degrees.

solve.work: The two remote interior angles sum to 130; equal, so 65 each.

questions.stem: An exterior angle at vertex $C$ of a triangle measures 100 degrees. The interior angles at $A$ and $B$ measure $2x$ and $3x$ degrees. How many degrees is the angle at $A$?
questions.solution: The exterior angle at $C$ equals the interior angles at $A$ and $B$ added: $5x=100$, so $x=20$. The angle at $A$ is $2x=40$ degrees.

questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, angle $B$ is $70^\circ$ and angle $C$ is $50^\circ$. Side $CA$ is extended beyond $A$. What does the exterior angle at $A$ (between the extension and side $AB$) measure?
questions.solution: The exterior angle at $A$ equals the sum of the two far interior angles: $70+50=120$ degrees. (Check: angle $A$ inside is $60^\circ$, and $60+120=180$.)

solve.work: Interior A = 180 - 70 - 50 = 60. Exterior at A = 180 - 60 = 120 (= B + C).

questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, the exterior angle at $B$ is 100 degrees larger than the interior angle at $B$. How many degrees is the interior angle at $B$?
questions.solution: The interior and exterior angles at $B$ add up to $180^\circ$. If the interior is $b$, then $b+(b+100)=180$, so $b=40$. (The exterior angle is $140^\circ$.)

questions.skill: Interior angle sum of a polygon
questions.stem: A convex polygon has 12 sides. What do its interior angles add up to, in degrees?
questions.solution: A polygon with $n$ sides has an angle sum of $(n-2)\times180$. With $n=12$ that is $10\times180=1800$ degrees.

questions.skill: Interior angle sum of a polygon
questions.stem: The interior angles of a polygon add up to 1260 degrees. How many sides does the polygon have?
questions.solution: The angle sum is $(n-2)\times180=1260$, so $n-2=7$ and $n=9$.

questions.skill: Interior angle sum of a polygon
questions.stem: A pentagon has angles of 100, 110 and 120 degrees, and its other two angles are equal. How many degrees is each of the two equal angles?
questions.solution: The pentagon's angles add up to $540^\circ$. The three known angles use $330^\circ$, leaving $210^\circ$ for the two equal angles. Each is $105$ degrees.

questions.skill: Interior angle sum of a polygon
questions.stem: Five of the angles of a hexagon each measure 130 degrees. How many degrees is the sixth angle?
questions.solution: A hexagon's angles add up to $720^\circ$. Five angles of $130^\circ$ use $650^\circ$, so the sixth angle is $720-650=70$ degrees.

questions.skill: Interior angle sum of a polygon
questions.stem: Which polygon has interior angles that add up to $1440^\circ$?
questions.solution: The angle sum is $(n-2)\times180=1440$, so $n-2=8$ and $n=10$. (Eight sides give 1080, nine give 1260 and twelve give 1800.)

questions.stem: How many degrees is each interior angle of a regular octagon?
questions.solution: The interior angles add up to $(8-2)\times180=1080$ degrees. Each of the 8 equal angles is $1080\div8=135$ degrees.

questions.stem: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon measures $40^\circ$. How many sides does the polygon have?
questions.solution: The exterior angles add up to $360^\circ$, so there are $360\div40=9$ sides.

questions.stem: Each interior angle of a regular polygon measures 150 degrees. How many sides does the polygon have?
questions.solution: Each exterior angle is $180-150=30$ degrees. The exterior angles add up to $360^\circ$, so there are $360\div30=12$ sides.

questions.stem: A hexagon has exterior angles of 40, 50, 60, 70 and 80 degrees at five of its corners, one exterior angle at each corner. How many degrees is the exterior angle at the sixth corner?
questions.solution: The six exterior angles add up to $360^\circ$. The five known ones add up to $300^\circ$, so the sixth is $360-300=60$ degrees.

questions.skill: Angle bisectors and angles around a point
questions.stem: Ray $OC$ lies inside angle $AOB$ and bisects it. Angle $AOC$ measures $(3x+4)^\circ$ and angle $COB$ measures $(5x-12)^\circ$. How many degrees is angle $AOB$?
questions.solution: A bisector makes equal halves: $3x+4=5x-12$, so $x=8$. Each half is $28^\circ$, so angle $AOB$ is $2\times28=56$ degrees.

questions.skill: Angle bisectors and angles around a point
questions.stem: Three angles around a point fill the whole turn. Their measures are in the ratio $2:3:4$. How many degrees is the largest angle?
questions.solution: The ratio parts total $2+3+4=9$, and the angles add to $360^\circ$, so one part is $40^\circ$. The largest angle is $4\times40=160$ degrees.

questions.skill: Angle bisectors and angles around a point
questions.stem: Angle $AOB$ measures 100 degrees. Ray $OC$ lies inside it so that angle $AOC$ is 30 degrees larger than angle $COB$. How many degrees is angle $COB$?
questions.solution: If $COB=c$, then $AOC=c+30$ and $c+c+30=100$, so $c=35$.

questions.skill: Angle bisectors and angles around a point
questions.stem: Rays $OA$ and $OB$ form an angle of 70 degrees, and ray $OC$ bisects it. Ray $OD$ points exactly opposite to $OC$, so that $C$, $O$ and $D$ lie on a straight line. How many degrees is angle $AOD$?
questions.solution: The bisector makes angle $AOC=35^\circ$. Angles $AOC$ and $AOD$ form a straight line, so angle $AOD=180-35=145$ degrees.

solve.work: AOC = 35. C, O, D collinear so AOC + AOD = 180, AOD = 145.

questions.stem: The supplement of an angle is 3 times its complement. How many degrees is the angle?
questions.solution: Let the angle be $a$. Then $180-a=3(90-a)=270-3a$, so $2a=90$ and $a=45$. Check: the supplement is $135^\circ$ and the complement is $45^\circ$; $135=3\times45$.

questions.stem: Lines $AB$ and $CD$ cross at $O$. Angle $AOC$ measures $(4x+10)^\circ$ and angle $AOD$ measures $(2x+20)^\circ$. What does angle $BOD$ measure?
questions.solution: Angles $AOC$ and $AOD$ form a straight line, so $4x+10+2x+20=180$, giving $x=25$. Angle $AOC=110^\circ$. Angle $BOD$ is vertical to $AOC$, so it is also 110 degrees.

solve.work: AOC and AOD form a straight line (OC, OD opposite): 4x+10 + 2x+20 = 180, x = 25. AOC = 110, AOD = 70. BOD is vertical to AOC, so 110.

questions.stem: An angle is 12 degrees less than one third of its supplement. How many degrees is the angle?
questions.solution: Let the angle be $a$. Then $a=\frac{180-a}{3}-12$. Multiply by 3: $3a=180-a-36$, so $4a=144$ and $a=36$. Check: the supplement is $144$, one third is $48$, and $48-12=36$.

questions.stem: Two angles are complementary and their measures are in the ratio $2:7$. What is the difference between the two angles? Answer in degrees.
questions.solution: The parts total $2+7=9$ and the angles add to $90^\circ$, so one part is $10^\circ$. The angles are $20^\circ$ and $70^\circ$, and they differ by 50 degrees.

questions.stem: Angle $b$ is acute. Angle $a$ is the complement of angle $b$, and angle $c$ is the supplement of angle $b$. How many degrees larger is angle $c$ than angle $a$?
questions.solution: We have $a=90-b$ and $c=180-b$. So $c-a=(180-b)-(90-b)=90$ degrees, whatever $b$ is.

questions.stem: A line crosses two parallel lines. Corresponding angles measure $(5x-12)^\circ$ and $(3x+16)^\circ$. How many degrees is the angle that forms a straight line with the $(5x-12)^\circ$ angle?
questions.solution: Corresponding angles are equal: $5x-12=3x+16$, so $x=14$ and each is $58^\circ$. The angle that forms a straight line with it is $180-58=122$ degrees.

solve.work: Corresponding angles equal: 5x - 12 = 3x + 16, x = 14, angle 58. Its linear pair: 180 - 58 = 122.

questions.stem: Lines $l$ and $m$ are parallel and are crossed by a transversal. A pair of alternate exterior angles measure $(4y+8)^\circ$ and $(6y-48)^\circ$. What is $y$?
questions.solution: Alternate exterior angles between parallel lines are equal: $4y+8=6y-48$, so $2y=56$ and $y=28$. (Each angle is $120^\circ$.)

questions.stem: Line $l$ is parallel to line $m$. Point $P$ is on $l$, and points $Q$ and $R$ are on $m$, below $l$. The angle between segment $PQ$ and line $l$, on the left of $P$, measures 50 degrees. The angle between segment $PR$ and line $l$, on the right of $P$, measures 65 degrees. How many degrees is angle $QPR$?
questions.solution: The two given angles and angle $QPR$ together fill the straight line $l$ at $P$: $50+QPR+65=180$, so $QPR=65$ degrees. (Check with alternate angles: angles $Q$ and $R$ of the triangle are $50^\circ$ and $65^\circ$, and $180-50-65=65$.)

solve.work: At P, the straight line l gives 50 + QPR + 65 = 180, so QPR = 65. (Equivalently alternate interior angles give PQR = 50, PRQ = 65, and the triangle sum gives 65.)

questions.stem: A line crosses two parallel lines. Two co-interior angles are such that one is 3 times the other. How many degrees is the larger of the two?
questions.solution: Co-interior angles add up to $180^\circ$. If the smaller is $s$, then $s+3s=180$, so $s=45$. The larger is $3\times45=135$ degrees.

questions.stem: A line crosses two parallel lines, making eight angles. One of them measures $x$ degrees. What is the sum of all eight angles, in degrees?
questions.solution: Four of the angles measure $x$ and the other four measure $180-x$. The sum is $4x+4(180-x)=720$ degrees, whatever $x$ is.

solve.work: At each crossing the four angles fill a full turn, 360. Two crossings: 720, whatever x is.

questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, angle $B$ is 20 degrees larger than angle $A$, and angle $C$ is twice angle $A$. How many degrees is angle $C$?
questions.solution: Let angle $A=a$. Then $B=a+20$ and $C=2a$. The sum is $4a+20=180$, so $a=40$. Angle $C=2\times40=80$ degrees.

questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, angle $A$ is $80^\circ$. The bisectors of angles $B$ and $C$ meet at point $I$. What does angle $BIC$ measure?
questions.solution: Angles $B$ and $C$ add up to $180-80=100$ degrees. Their halves add up to $50^\circ$. In triangle $BIC$ the third angle is $180-50=130$ degrees.

questions.stem: Triangle $ABC$ has angle $B=40^\circ$ and angle $C=60^\circ$. Point $D$ is on side $BC$ with $AD$ perpendicular to $BC$. Point $E$ is on $BC$ with $AE$ bisecting angle $A$. How many degrees is angle $DAE$?
questions.solution: Angle $A=180-40-60=80^\circ$, so $AE$ makes angle $BAE=40^\circ$. In right triangle $ABD$, angle $BAD=90-40=50^\circ$. So angle $DAE=50-40=10$ degrees.

solve.work: A = 80, BAE = 40. In right triangle ABD, BAD = 90 - 40 = 50. DAE = 50 - 40 = 10.

questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, angle $A$ is 20 degrees less than the sum of angles $B$ and $C$. How many degrees is angle $A$?
questions.solution: Angles $B$ and $C$ add up to $180-A$. So $A=(180-A)-20$, giving $2A=160$ and $A=80$ degrees.

questions.stem: One angle of an isosceles triangle measures $100^\circ$. Which gives the other two angles?
questions.solution: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles. They cannot both be $100^\circ$ (that is already $200^\circ$), so $100^\circ$ is the apex and the two equal base angles share the other $80^\circ$: $40^\circ$ each.

solve.work: 100 cannot be a base angle (two would exceed 180), so it is the apex: base angles (180 - 100)/2 = 40 each.

questions.stem: A triangle has one exterior angle at each corner. At corners $A$ and $B$ the exterior angles measure 130 degrees and 110 degrees. How many degrees is the interior angle at $C$?
questions.solution: The interior angle at $A$ is $180-130=50^\circ$ and at $B$ is $180-110=70^\circ$. So the angle at $C$ is $180-50-70=60$ degrees.

questions.stem: An exterior angle of a triangle measures $150^\circ$. The two interior angles that are not next to it are in the ratio $2:3$. What does the larger of them measure?
questions.solution: The two far interior angles add up to the exterior angle, $150^\circ$. In the ratio $2:3$ they are $60^\circ$ and $90^\circ$. The larger is 90 degrees.

questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, side $AB$ is extended beyond $B$ to a point $D$, and angle $CBD$ measures 110 degrees. Angle $A$ is 20 degrees larger than angle $C$. How many degrees is angle $C$?
questions.solution: Angle $CBD$ is an exterior angle, so $A+C=110$. With $A=C+20$: $2C+20=110$, so $C=45$ degrees (and $A=65^\circ$).

solve.work: CBD is the exterior angle at B, = A + C = 110. A = C + 20, so 2C + 20 = 110, C = 45.

questions.stem: The three exterior angles of a triangle (one at each corner) are in the ratio $3:4:5$. How many degrees is the smallest interior angle of the triangle?
