questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, $AB < BC < CA$. Which list gives the angles from smallest to largest?
questions.solution: $\angle C$ is opposite $AB$ (the shortest side), $\angle A$ is opposite $BC$ and $\angle B$ is opposite $CA$ (the longest side). So from smallest to largest: $\angle C, \angle A, \angle B$.

solve.work: AB opposite C, BC opposite A, CA opposite B; so C < A < B.

questions.skill: Angles from the sides: the largest angle is opposite the longest side
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, $AB = 8$ and $BC = 11$, and $\angle B$ is the largest of the three angles. The length of $CA$ is a whole number. How many values could it have?
questions.solution: The side opposite the largest angle is the longest side, so $CA$ is longer than $11$. By the triangle inequality $CA < 8 + 11 = 19$. The whole numbers from $12$ to $18$ give $7$ values.

solve.work: B largest means CA (opposite B) is the longest side, CA > 11, and CA < 8+11 = 19: 12..18 -> 7 values.

questions.skill: Sides from the angles: the longest side is opposite the largest angle
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, $\angle A = 35^\circ$ and $\angle B = 75^\circ$. Which side is the shortest?
choices: There are two shortest sides of equal length
questions.solution: The third angle is $\angle C = 180 - 35 - 75 = 70^\circ$. The smallest angle is $\angle A = 35^\circ$, and the side opposite it, $BC$, is the shortest.

solve.work: C = 70; A = 35 smallest, so BC is shortest.

questions.skill: Sides from the angles: the longest side is opposite the largest angle
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, $\angle A$ is twice $\angle B$, and $\angle C$ is three times $\angle B$. Which side is the longest?
questions.solution: Let $\angle B = x$. Then $x + 2x + 3x = 180$, so $x = 30^\circ$, $\angle A = 60^\circ$ and $\angle C = 90^\circ$. The largest angle is $\angle C$, and the side opposite it is $AB$.

solve.work: B + 2B + 3B = 180, B = 30, A = 60, C = 90. Longest is opposite C: AB.

questions.skill: Sides from the angles: the longest side is opposite the largest angle
questions.stem: The angles $\angle A$, $\angle B$ and $\angle C$ of a triangle are in the ratio $3 : 5 : 4$. Which list gives the sides from shortest to longest?
questions.solution: The ratio has $12$ parts of $15^\circ$ each, so $\angle A = 45^\circ$, $\angle B = 75^\circ$ and $\angle C = 60^\circ$. The sides opposite them are $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ respectively, so from smallest angle to largest the sides are $BC, AB, CA$.

solve.work: A = 45, B = 75, C = 60. Opposite A: BC, opposite C: AB, opposite B: CA. Shortest to longest: BC, AB, CA.

questions.stem: Towns $A$, $B$ and $C$ do not lie on one straight line. $AB = 8$ km and $BC = 5$ km. Which of these could be the straight-line distance $AC$, in kilometers?
questions.solution: Since $A$, $B$ and $C$ form a triangle, $AC$ is greater than $8 - 5 = 3$ and less than $8 + 5 = 13$. Only $12$ is strictly in that range.

questions.stem: Point $P$ is 9 units from point $Q$, and point $R$ is 5 units from $P$. The points may be on one line or not. What is the greatest possible distance $QR$?
questions.solution: $QR$ is never more than the path through $P$, which is $9 + 5 = 14$. It equals $14$ when $P$ is between $Q$ and $R$ on a line, so the greatest possible distance is $14$.

solve.work: Maximum when collinear with P between Q and R: 9+5 = 14.

questions.stem: Towns $A$, $B$ and $C$ do not lie on one straight line. A road goes straight from $A$ to $C$, which is 12 km, and then straight from $C$ to $B$, which is 8 km. Which statement about the straight-line distance $AB$ is true?
choices: $AB$ is greater than 4 km and less than 20 km
$AB$ is exactly 20 km, the length of the route
$AB$ is greater than 20 km, the route being a detour
$AB$ is at least 12 km but at most 20 km
questions.answer: $AB$ is greater than 4 km and less than 20 km
questions.solution: Because $A$, $B$ and $C$ form a triangle, $AB$ is less than $12 + 8 = 20$ and greater than $12 - 8 = 4$.

solve.answer: $AB$ is greater than 4 km and less than 20 km

questions.skill: Perimeter of a triangle: bounds and possible values
questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle are 9 cm and 12 cm, and the third side is a whole number of centimeters. What is the least possible perimeter, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The third side must be greater than $12 - 9 = 3$, so its least value is $4$. The least perimeter is $9 + 12 + 4 = 25$ cm.

questions.skill: Perimeter of a triangle: bounds and possible values
questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle are 10 and 15. Which of these is NOT possible for the perimeter of the triangle?
questions.solution: The third side is between $5$ and $25$, so the perimeter is between $30$ and $50$, not including either end. The values $31$, $40$ and $49$ fit. A perimeter of $50$ would need a third side of $25$, which equals $10 + 15$ and makes the triangle flat.

questions.skill: Perimeter of a triangle: bounds and possible values
questions.stem: A triangle has sides of 8, 11 and $x$, where $x$ is a whole number. For how many values of $x$ is the perimeter a multiple of 5?
questions.solution: The third side is between $3$ and $19$, so $x$ is $4, 5, \ldots, 18$. The perimeter is $19 + x$, a multiple of $5$ when $x$ is $1$ more than a multiple of $5$: $x = 6, 11, 16$. That is $3$ values.

solve.work: 3 < x < 19, x = 4..18. Perimeter 19 + x multiple of 5 -> x = 6, 11, 16: 3.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides of lengths $x$, $2x$ and 15, where $x$ is a whole number. How many values of $x$ are possible?
questions.solution: Three conditions: $x + 2x > 15$ gives $x > 5$; $x + 15 > 2x$ gives $x < 15$; and $2x + 15 > x$ is always true. So $x = 6, 7, \ldots, 14$, which is $9$ values.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides of lengths 8, $2x$ and 12. Which describes all the possible values of $x$?
questions.solution: The side $2x$ must be greater than $12 - 8 = 4$ and less than $12 + 8 = 20$. Dividing by $2$ gives $2 < x < 10$. The option $4 < x < 20$ describes $2x$, not $x$.

questions.skill: Can three lengths form a triangle?
questions.stem: Sara has five sticks, of lengths $3$, $5$, $7$, $11$ and $15$ centimeters. She picks three of the sticks and tries to make a triangle with them. For how many different choices of three sticks is this possible?
questions.solution: There are $10$ choices of three sticks. The ones that work (the two shorter sticks add to more than the longest) are: $3,5,7$ since $8>7$; $5,7,11$ since $12>11$; $5,11,15$ since $16>15$; and $7,11,15$ since $18>15$. All the other choices that use the $3$ centimeter stick fail. So the answer is $4$.

questions.stem: An isosceles triangle has two sides of lengths $6$ and $15$. What is its perimeter?
questions.solution: Either the equal sides are $6$ and $6$ with a base of $15$, or the equal sides are $15$ and $15$ with a base of $6$. The first would need $6+6>15$, which is false. So the sides are $15$, $15$ and $6$, and the perimeter is $15+15+6=36$.

questions.stem: How many different triangles with whole-number side lengths have a perimeter of $13$? Count triangles with the same three side lengths as one.
questions.solution: List the sides from shortest to longest, $a\le b\le c$, with $a+b+c=13$ and $a+b>c$, so $c\le 6$. With $c=5$: $3,5,5$ and $4,4,5$. With $c=6$: $1,6,6$ and $2,5,6$ and $3,4,6$. A longest side of $4$ or less cannot reach a perimeter of $13$, and one of $7$ or more fails the triangle inequality. That gives $5$ triangles.

questions.skill: Angles from the sides: the largest angle is opposite the longest side
questions.stem: A triangle has sides of lengths $x$, $x + 3$ and $2x - 1$ centimeters, and its perimeter is $30$ centimeters. How long is the side that is opposite the largest angle, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The perimeter is $x+(x+3)+(2x-1)=4x+2=30$, so $x=7$ and the sides are $7$, $10$ and $13$. The largest angle is opposite the longest side, which is $13$ centimeters.

solve.work: x + x + 3 + 2x - 1 = 4x + 2 = 30, x = 7. Sides 7, 10, 13 (valid: 17 > 13). Largest angle is opposite the longest side, 13.

questions.skill: Sides from the angles: the longest side is opposite the largest angle
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, $AB = AC$ and $\angle A = 40^\circ$. Which statement is true?
questions.solution: The equal sides give equal angles opposite them: $\angle B=\angle C=(180-40)\div 2=70^\circ$. The smallest angle is $\angle A=40^\circ$, and the side opposite it is $BC$, so $BC$ is the shortest side. $AB=AC$ is given, and the triangle is not equilateral.

solve.work: Angles B = C = 70, A = 40 is the smallest, so BC (opposite A) is the shortest side.

questions.skill: Perimeter of a triangle: bounds and possible values
questions.stem: A triangle has whole-number side lengths and a perimeter of $30$. What is the greatest possible length of one of its sides?
questions.solution: Any side must be shorter than the sum of the other two, so it is shorter than half the perimeter: less than $30\div 2=15$. As a whole number, a side can be at most $14$, for example in the triangle $14, 14, 2$ or $14, 9, 7$ ($9+7=16>14$).

solve.work: Longest side c < 30 - c, so c < 15, c <= 14. 14, 14, 2 (or 14, 8, 8) works. Answer 14.

questions.skill: Perimeter of a triangle: bounds and possible values
questions.stem: A triangle has a perimeter of $36$. Which of these could be the length of its longest side?
questions.solution: The longest side is at least a third of the perimeter, $36\div 3=12$, and it must be shorter than half the perimeter, $36\div 2=18$. Of the choices only $15$ lies in that range, and it works: for example $15, 12, 9$ has $12+9=21>15$. A longest side of $10$ is too short to reach a perimeter of $36$, and $18$ or $20$ is too long.

solve.work: Longest side c: c < 36 - c so c < 18, and c >= 36/3 = 12. Of 15, 18, 10, 20 only 15 works (e.g. 15, 12, 9). 10 cannot be the longest (sum would be at most 30).

questions.stem: Ana lives $7$ kilometers from the library and Ben lives $12$ kilometers from the library, both measured in a straight line. The library and the two homes may or may not lie on one straight line. What is the difference between the greatest and the least possible straight-line distance between Ana and Ben, in kilometers?
questions.solution: The distance between the homes is at most $12+7=19$ (when the library is between them on a line) and at least $12-7=5$ (when they are on the same side of it on a line). The difference is $19-5=14$ kilometers.

solve.work: Collinear allowed: distance ranges from 12 - 7 = 5 to 12 + 7 = 19. Difference 14.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides of lengths $x$, $x + 5$ and $3x - 1$, where $x$ is a whole number. For how many values of $x$ does such a triangle exist?
questions.solution: Need each side shorter than the sum of the other two. From $x+(x+5)>3x-1$ we get $x<6$. From $x+(3x-1)>x+5$ we get $x>2$. The third condition always holds. So $x=3,4,5$, which is $3$ values. (At $x=2$ and $x=6$ the triangle is flat.)

questions.stem: A triangle has sides of lengths $6$, $x$ and $14 - x$. Which describes all the possible values of $x$?
questions.solution: Two conditions matter. First, $6+x>14-x$ gives $2x>8$, so $x>4$. Second, $6+(14-x)>x$ gives $20>2x$, so $x<10$. The third condition, $x+(14-x)=14>6$, always holds. So $4<x<10$, with the ends excluded because they make flat triangles.

solve.work: x + (14 - x) = 14 > 6 always. 6 + x > 14 - x gives x > 4. 6 + 14 - x > x gives x < 10. So 4 < x < 10.

questions.skill: Can three lengths form a triangle?
questions.stem: Six sticks are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 cm long. How many different groups of three of these sticks can be the sides of a triangle?
questions.solution: Sort each group as $a < b < c$ and test $a + b > c$. With $c = 4$: $2, 3, 4$ works. With $c = 5$: $2, 4, 5$ and $3, 4, 5$ work. With $c = 6$: $2, 5, 6$; $3, 4, 6$; $3, 5, 6$ and $4, 5, 6$ work. With $c = 3$ nothing works ($1 + 2 = 3$). The total is $1 + 2 + 4 = 7$.

questions.skill: Can three lengths form a triangle?
questions.stem: Which statement is true for every positive number $x$, about three sticks of lengths $x$, $x$ and $2x$?
choices: They can never form a triangle
They form a triangle only when $x$ is greater than 2
They form a triangle only when $x$ is a whole number
questions.answer: They can never form a triangle
questions.solution: The two shorter sticks add up to $x + x = 2x$, which equals the longest stick and is never greater than it. So the sticks would lie flat along a line, whatever $x$ is.

solve.answer: They can never form a triangle
solve.work: x + x = 2x, not greater than 2x: never a triangle.

questions.skill: Can three lengths form a triangle?
questions.stem: For how many whole numbers $k$ from 1 to 20 can sticks of 5 cm, 12 cm and $k$ cm NOT form a triangle?
questions.solution: The third stick must be longer than $12 - 5 = 7$ and shorter than $12 + 5 = 17$, so $k = 8, 9, \ldots, 16$ works, which is $9$ values. The other $20 - 9 = 11$ values of $k$ do not work.

solve.work: Triangle iff 7 < k < 17: k = 8..16 (9 values). Not a triangle: 20-9 = 11.

questions.stem: The possible lengths of the third side of a triangle are exactly the numbers $x$ with $5 < x < 15$. What is the length of the longer of the other two sides?
questions.solution: If the other two sides are $m > n$, the possible lengths are $m - n < x < m + n$. So $m - n = 5$ and $m + n = 15$. Adding gives $2m = 20$, so $m = 10$ (and $n = 5$).

questions.stem: A triangle has two sides of lengths 9 and 14 and is isosceles. What is the sum of its two possible perimeters?
questions.solution: The third side equals one of the given sides. If it is $9$ the sides are $9, 9, 14$ and $9 + 9 > 14$, so this is a triangle with perimeter $32$. If it is $14$ the sides are $9, 14, 14$ with perimeter $37$. The sum is $32 + 37 = 69$.

questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle have lengths $s$ and $2s$, where $s$ is a positive number. Which describes all the possible lengths $x$ of the third side?
questions.solution: The third side is greater than $2s - s = s$ and less than $2s + s = 3s$.

questions.stem: How many different triangles with whole-number side lengths have a longest side of length 6? Triangles with the same three side lengths count as one.
questions.solution: Write the sides as $a \le b \le 6$ with $a + b > 6$. For $b = 6$: $a = 1, \ldots, 6$ gives $6$. For $b = 5$: $a = 2, \ldots, 5$ gives $4$. For $b = 4$: $a = 3, 4$ gives $2$. For $b \le 3$ nothing works. The total is $12$.

questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle are 12 and 20, and the third side is a whole number. How many of its possible lengths are even?
questions.solution: The third side is greater than $8$ and less than $32$, so it is a whole number from $9$ to $31$. The even ones are $10, 12, \ldots, 30$, which is $11$ numbers.

questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle add up to 16 and differ by 6. The third side is a whole number. How many different lengths could it have?
questions.solution: The two sides are $11$ and $5$. The third side is greater than $11 - 5 = 6$ and less than $11 + 5 = 16$, so it is $7, 8, \ldots, 15$, which is $9$ lengths.

questions.skill: Angles from the sides: the largest angle is opposite the longest side
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, $AB = 6$ and $AC = 8$, and $\angle A$ is the largest angle. The length of $BC$ is a whole number. How many values could it have?
questions.solution: The side opposite the largest angle is the longest, so $BC > 8$. By the triangle inequality $BC < 6 + 8 = 14$. The whole numbers from $9$ to $13$ give $5$ values.

solve.work: A largest means BC is the longest side: BC > 8, BC < 14: 9..13 -> 5.

questions.skill: Angles from the sides: the largest angle is opposite the longest side
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, $AB = 10$ and the angles satisfy $\angle C > \angle B > \angle A$. The lengths of $BC$ and $CA$ are whole numbers. What is the greatest possible length of $BC$?
questions.solution: $\angle C$ is the largest angle, so $AB = 10$ is the longest side. $\angle B > \angle A$ means the side opposite $\angle B$, which is $CA$, is longer than the side opposite $\angle A$, which is $BC$. So $BC < CA < 10$. The greatest whole numbers are $BC = 8$, $CA = 9$, and $8 + 9 > 10$ so this is a triangle.

solve.work: C > B > A gives AB > CA > BC, with AB = 10. BC < CA <= 9, so BC <= 8; BC = 8, CA = 9 works (17 > 10).

questions.skill: Sides from the angles: the longest side is opposite the largest angle
questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, $\angle A = 30^\circ$ and $\angle B$ is twice $\angle C$. Which side is the longest?
questions.solution: $\angle B + \angle C = 150^\circ$ and $\angle B = 2\angle C$, so $\angle C = 50^\circ$ and $\angle B = 100^\circ$. The largest angle is $\angle B$, and the side opposite it is $CA$.

solve.work: B + C = 150, B = 2C -> C = 50, B = 100. Longest is opposite B: CA.

questions.skill: Sides from the angles: the longest side is opposite the largest angle
questions.stem: In triangle $PQR$, $\angle P < \angle Q < \angle R$. The sides $PQ$, $QR$ and $RP$ have lengths that are three consecutive whole numbers, and the perimeter is 15. What is the length of $QR$?
questions.solution: Three consecutive numbers with sum $15$ are $4, 5, 6$. The smallest angle, $\angle P$, is opposite $QR$, so $QR$ is the shortest side, $4$.

solve.work: Sides 4, 5, 6. P is smallest, so QR (opposite P) is shortest: 4.

questions.skill: Sides from the angles: the longest side is opposite the largest angle
questions.stem: The exterior angle at $A$ of triangle $ABC$ (formed by extending side $BA$ beyond $A$) is $100^\circ$, and $\angle B = 60^\circ$. Which side is the shortest?
choices: No side is shorter than the others
questions.solution: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two far interior angles, so $\angle B + \angle C = 100$ and $\angle C = 40^\circ$. Then $\angle A = 180 - 100 = 80^\circ$. The smallest angle is $\angle C = 40^\circ$, and the side opposite it is $AB$.

solve.work: Angle A = 180-100 = 80, B = 60, C = 40. Shortest is opposite C: AB.

questions.stem: Point $P$ is 9 units from point $Q$, and point $R$ is 4 units from $P$. The three points do not lie on one line, and the distance $QR$ is a whole number. How many values could $QR$ have?
questions.solution: $P$, $Q$ and $R$ form a triangle, so $QR$ is greater than $9 - 4 = 5$ and less than $9 + 4 = 13$. The whole numbers $6, 7, \ldots, 12$ give $7$ values.

questions.stem: Points $P$ and $Q$ are a whole number $d$ of units apart. Point $M$ is 7 units from $P$ and 12 units from $Q$, and the three points do not lie on one line. How many values of $d$ are possible?
questions.solution: $P$, $Q$ and $M$ form a triangle with two sides $7$ and $12$, so $d$ is greater than $12 - 7 = 5$ and less than $12 + 7 = 19$. The whole numbers $6, 7, \ldots, 18$ give $13$ values.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$ and $C$ lie on one straight line. $AB = 5$ and $BC = 9$. Which of these could be the length $AC$?
questions.solution: On a line, $C$ is either on the same side of $B$ as $A$ or on the other side, so $AC = 9 - 5 = 4$ or $AC = 9 + 5 = 14$. Only $4$ is on the list. A length such as $7$ would be possible only if the points were not on one line.

solve.work: Collinear: AC = 9+5 = 14 or 9-5 = 4. Only 4 is offered.

questions.skill: Perimeter of a triangle: bounds and possible values
questions.stem: A triangle has whole-number sides, a perimeter of 25 and a longest side of 11. How many different triangles are possible? Triangles with the same three side lengths count as one.
questions.solution: The other two sides $a \le b \le 11$ add up to $14$, and the triangle inequality $a + b = 14 > 11$ already holds. So $b$ runs from $7$ to $11$ (with $a = 14 - b$): $7,7$; $6,8$; $5,9$; $4,10$; $3,11$. That is $5$ triangles.

questions.skill: Perimeter of a triangle: bounds and possible values
questions.stem: A triangle has three different whole-number side lengths and a perimeter of 12. What is the length of its longest side?
questions.solution: The longest side is less than half the perimeter, so it is less than $6$. With the longest side $5$, the others add up to $7$ and are different and shorter: $3$ and $4$. With $4$ the others add to $8$ but would have to be shorter than $4$ and different, which is impossible. The triangle is $3, 4, 5$.

solve.work: a < b < c, a + b + c = 12, c < 6. c = 5: a + b = 7 with b < 5 -> (3,4). Triangle 3, 4, 5; longest 5.

questions.skill: Perimeter of a triangle: bounds and possible values
questions.stem: A triangle has perimeter $P$. Which describes all the possible lengths $L$ of its longest side?
questions.solution: The longest side is at least the average side, $\frac{P}{3}$, and it equals that only in an equilateral triangle, so $\frac{P}{3}$ is allowed. The longest side is less than the sum of the other two, so $L < P - L$ and $L < \frac{P}{2}$.

solve.work: L < P - L gives L < P/2; L is at least the average, L >= P/3, equality for equilateral.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides of lengths $x$, $2x + 1$ and $20 - x$, where $x$ is a whole number. How many values of $x$ are possible?
questions.solution: Test each way. $x + (2x + 1) > 20 - x$ gives $4x > 19$, so $x \ge 5$. $x + (20 - x) > 2x + 1$ gives $20 > 2x + 1$, so $x \le 9$. The third condition, $(2x + 1) + (20 - x) > x$, always holds. So $x = 5, 6, 7, 8, 9$, which is $5$ values.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides of lengths $x$, $x + 2$ and $3x - 4$. Which describes all the possible values of $x$?
questions.solution: We need $x + (x + 2) > 3x - 4$, which gives $x < 6$, and $x + (3x - 4) > x + 2$, which gives $3x > 6$ and $x > 2$. The third condition, $(x + 2) + (3x - 4) > x$, gives $x > \frac{2}{3}$, which $x > 2$ already covers, and all sides are positive when $x > 2$. So $2 < x < 6$.

solve.work: x + x + 2 > 3x - 4 -> x < 6; x + 3x - 4 > x + 2 -> x > 2; 4x - 2 > x -> x > 2/3. So 2 < x < 6 (sides then positive).

questions.stem: A triangle has sides of lengths $x$, $14 - x$ and 14. Which statement is true?
choices: No such triangle exists for any value of $x$
A triangle exists for every $x$ with $0 < x < 14$
A triangle exists for every $x$ with $7 < x < 14$
questions.answer: No such triangle exists for any value of $x$
questions.solution: The first two sides add up to $x + (14 - x) = 14$, which equals the third side and is never greater than it. So the three lengths can never form a triangle.

solve.answer: No such triangle exists for any value of $x$
solve.work: x + (14 - x) = 14 is never greater than 14, so no triangle exists.

questions.stem: A round table has a diameter of 1.2 meters. What is the radius of the table, in meters?
questions.solution: The radius is half the diameter: $1.2 \div 2 = 0.6$ meters.

questions.stem: Which statement about a circle is true?
choices: A radius is twice as long as a diameter.
Every chord is as long as a diameter.
A diameter is twice as long as a radius.
Every chord passes through the center.
questions.answer: A diameter is twice as long as a radius.
questions.solution: A diameter is a chord through the center, and it is made of two radii, so it is twice as long as a radius. A chord that does not pass through the center is shorter than a diameter, so the other statements are false.

solve.answer: A diameter is twice as long as a radius.
solve.work: A diameter is two radii, so it is twice a radius: true. Not every chord passes through the centre, a radius is not twice a diameter, and only diameters are as long as a diameter.

questions.stem: A circular pond has a radius of 5 meters. The distance around the pond is $k\pi$ meters. What is $k$?
questions.solution: The circumference of a circle is $2\pi r$. With $r = 5$ it is $2 \times 5 \times \pi = 10\pi$, so $k = 10$.

questions.stem: A circle has a diameter of 12 inches. What is its circumference, in inches?
questions.solution: The circumference is $\pi$ times the diameter: $\pi \times 12 = 12\pi$ inches. ($6\pi$ forgets the 2 in $2\pi r$, $24\pi$ uses the diameter as the radius, and $36\pi$ is the area $\pi r^2$ with $r = 6$.)

questions.stem: A round coaster has a radius of 4 cm. The area of its top is $k\pi$ square centimeters. What is $k$?
questions.solution: The area of a circle is $\pi r^2$. With $r = 4$ it is $\pi \times 4^2 = 16\pi$, so $k = 16$.

questions.stem: A circular rug has a diameter of 10 feet. What is its area, in square feet?
questions.solution: The radius is $10 \div 2 = 5$ feet, so the area is $\pi r^2 = 25\pi$ square feet. ($100\pi$ uses the diameter as the radius, and $10\pi$ is the circumference.)

questions.stem: A circle has a circumference of 40 cm. An arc of this circle has a central angle of $90^\circ$. How long is the arc, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The arc is $\frac{90}{360} = \frac{1}{4}$ of the whole circle, so its length is $\frac{1}{4} \times 40 = 10$ cm.

questions.stem: A circle has an area of $36\pi$ square inches. A sector makes up one quarter of the circle. What is the area of the sector?
questions.solution: A sector that is one quarter of the circle has one quarter of the area: $36\pi \div 4 = 9\pi$ square inches.

questions.stem: A line through the center of a circle is perpendicular to a chord that is 14 cm long. The line cuts the chord into two pieces. How long is each piece, in centimeters?
questions.solution: A line from the center that is perpendicular to a chord cuts the chord in half. Each piece is $14 \div 2 = 7$ cm.

solve.work: A line through the centre perpendicular to a chord bisects it: 14/2 = 7.

questions.stem: A line touches a circle at exactly one point, $T$. The center of the circle is $O$. What is the measure of the angle between $\overline{OT}$ and the line?
questions.solution: A tangent line is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point where it touches the circle, so the angle is $90^\circ$.

solve.work: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency: 90 degrees.

questions.stem: A circle has a radius of 7.5 cm. What is its diameter, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The diameter is twice the radius, so it is $2 \times 7.5 = 15$ cm.

questions.stem: A circle has a diameter of 18 inches. What is its radius, in inches?
questions.solution: The radius is half the diameter: $18 \div 2 = 9$ inches.

questions.stem: Which is the longest chord of a circle?
choices: A chord that does not pass through the center
All chords of a circle have the same length
questions.solution: A chord through the center is a diameter, and no chord is longer than a diameter. A radius is not a chord (it has only one end on the circle), a chord that misses the center is shorter than a diameter, and chords differ in length.

solve.work: A chord through the center (a diameter) is the longest chord; a radius is not a chord.

questions.stem: A circle has a diameter of 9 cm. Its circumference is $k\pi$ centimeters. What is $k$?
questions.solution: The circumference is $\pi \times \text{diameter} = 9\pi$, so $k = 9$.

questions.stem: A circle has a radius of 6 inches. What is its circumference, in inches?
questions.solution: The circumference is $2\pi r = 2\pi \times 6 = 12\pi$ inches.

questions.stem: A circle has a circumference of $30\pi$ meters. What is its diameter, in meters?
questions.solution: The circumference is $\pi \times \text{diameter}$, so the diameter is $30\pi \div \pi = 30$ meters.

solve.work: C = pi d, 30pi = pi d, d = 30.

questions.stem: A circle has a radius of 9 cm. Its area is $k\pi$ square centimeters. What is $k$?
questions.solution: The area is $\pi r^2 = \pi \times 9^2 = 81\pi$, so $k = 81$.

questions.stem: A circle has a radius of 3 meters. What is its area, in square meters?
questions.solution: The area is $\pi r^2 = \pi \times 3^2 = 9\pi$ square meters. ($6\pi$ is the circumference, not the area.)

questions.stem: A circle has an area of $49\pi$ square meters. What is its radius, in meters?
questions.solution: The area is $\pi r^2 = 49\pi$, so $r^2 = 49$ and $r = 7$ meters.

questions.stem: A central angle of $180^\circ$ cuts off an arc of a circle. What fraction of the circumference is that arc?
questions.solution: A full circle is $360^\circ$, and $\frac{180}{360} = \frac{1}{2}$, so the arc is half of the circumference.

questions.stem: A circle has a circumference of 24 cm. An arc of the circle has a central angle of $60^\circ$. How long is the arc, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The arc is $\frac{60}{360} = \frac{1}{6}$ of the circumference: $24 \div 6 = 4$ cm.

questions.stem: An arc is one-fifth of a circle. What is the measure of its central angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: One-fifth of $360^\circ$ is $360 \div 5 = 72^\circ$.

questions.stem: A circle has an area of 80 square centimeters. A sector of the circle has a central angle of $90^\circ$. What is the area of the sector, in square centimeters?
questions.solution: $90^\circ$ is $\frac{1}{4}$ of $360^\circ$, so the sector is a quarter of the circle: $80 \div 4 = 20$ square centimeters.

questions.stem: A circle with an area of $20\pi$ square centimeters is cut into 5 sectors of equal size. What is the area of one sector?
questions.solution: Each sector is one-fifth of the circle: $20\pi \div 5 = 4\pi$ square centimeters.

questions.stem: A sector of a circle has a central angle of $45^\circ$. How many sectors of this size fit together to make the whole circle?
questions.solution: The whole circle is $360^\circ$, and $360 \div 45 = 8$.

questions.stem: Chord $AB$ of a circle is 20 cm long. A line from the center $O$, perpendicular to $AB$, meets it at $M$. How long is $AM$, in centimeters?
questions.solution: A line from the center that is perpendicular to a chord cuts the chord in half. So $AM = 20 \div 2 = 10$ cm.

solve.work: The perpendicular from the center bisects the chord, so AM = 20/2 = 10.

questions.stem: A line segment from the center of a circle is perpendicular to a chord. Which statement is true?
choices: It is always as long as the radius.
It makes a $45^\circ$ angle with the chord.
It is always the same length as the chord.
It cuts the chord into two equal pieces.
questions.answer: It cuts the chord into two equal pieces.
questions.solution: A perpendicular from the center to a chord always bisects the chord. The segment meets the chord at $90^\circ$, not $45^\circ$, and its length depends on how far the chord is from the center, so it is not always the radius or the chord's length.

solve.answer: It cuts the chord into two equal pieces.
solve.work: A perpendicular from the center to a chord bisects the chord. The other statements are false in general.

questions.stem: In a circle with center $O$, the segment from $O$ perpendicular to chord $AB$ meets it at $M$. If $AM = 5.5$ cm, how long is chord $AB$, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The perpendicular from the center bisects the chord, so $AB = 2 \times AM = 2 \times 5.5 = 11$ cm.

solve.work: M is the midpoint, so AB = 2(5.5) = 11.

questions.stem: A line is tangent to a circle. How many points do the line and the circle have in common?
questions.solution: A tangent line touches the circle at one point only. A line with two common points cuts through the circle (a secant).

solve.work: A tangent line meets the circle in exactly one point.

questions.stem: From a point $P$ outside a circle, two tangent segments $\overline{PA}$ and $\overline{PB}$ touch the circle at $A$ and $B$. If $PA = 9$ cm, how long is $PB$, in centimeters?
questions.solution: Tangent segments drawn from the same outside point to a circle are equal in length, so $PB = PA = 9$ cm.

solve.work: Tangent segments from an external point are equal: PB = PA = 9.

questions.stem: The line $PT$ is tangent to a circle with center $O$ at the point $T$. In triangle $OTP$, which angle is a right angle?
choices: None of the angles has to be a right angle
questions.solution: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of tangency, so $\overline{OT} \perp \overline{PT}$ and $\angle OTP = 90^\circ$.

solve.work: The radius to the point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent, so the right angle is at T: angle OTP.

questions.stem: One circle has a radius of 3 cm. A second circle has a diameter of 10 cm. How many centimeters longer is the radius of the second circle than the radius of the first?
questions.solution: The second circle has radius $10 \div 2 = 5$ cm. Then $5 - 3 = 2$ cm.

questions.stem: Point $O$ is the center of a circle, and $A$ and $B$ are points on the circle. If $OA = 6$ cm, how long is $OB$, in centimeters?
questions.solution: Every point on a circle is the same distance from the center, so $OB = OA = 6$ cm.

solve.work: All radii are equal: OB = OA = 6.

questions.stem: A circular garden has a circumference of $18\pi$ meters. What is the radius of the garden, in meters?
questions.solution: The circumference is $2\pi r$. So $2\pi r = 18\pi$, which gives $r = 18 \div 2 = 9$ meters.

questions.stem: A circle has a circumference of $16\pi$. What is the area of the circle?
questions.solution: From $2\pi r = 16\pi$ we get $r = 8$. The area is $\pi r^2 = 64\pi$.

questions.stem: In a circle of radius 10 cm, an arc has a central angle of $72^\circ$. The length of the arc is $k\pi$ centimeters. What is $k$?
questions.solution: The whole circumference is $2\pi \times 10 = 20\pi$. The arc is $\frac{72}{360} = \frac{1}{5}$ of the circle, so its length is $\frac{1}{5} \times 20\pi = 4\pi$, and $k = 4$.

questions.stem: An arc of length $6\pi$ belongs to a circle of radius $12$. What is the central angle of the arc?
questions.solution: The whole circumference is $2\pi \times 12 = 24\pi$. The arc is $\frac{6\pi}{24\pi} = \frac{1}{4}$ of the circle, so its central angle is $\frac{1}{4} \times 360^\circ = 90^\circ$.

questions.stem: A sector of a circle of radius 6 cm has a central angle of $60^\circ$. The area of the sector is $k\pi$ square centimeters. What is $k$?
questions.solution: The whole circle has area $\pi \times 6^2 = 36\pi$. The sector is $\frac{60}{360} = \frac{1}{6}$ of the circle, so its area is $\frac{1}{6} \times 36\pi = 6\pi$, and $k = 6$.

questions.stem: A pizza with a diameter of 16 inches is cut into 8 slices of equal size. What is the area of one slice, in square inches?
questions.solution: The radius is 8 inches, so the whole pizza has area $\pi \times 8^2 = 64\pi$. One slice is $\frac{1}{8}$ of that: $8\pi$ square inches. ($2\pi$ would be the length of the curved edge of one slice.)

questions.stem: A chord of a circle is 16 cm long and is 6 cm from the center of the circle. What is the radius of the circle, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The perpendicular from the center to the chord cuts it in half, giving a right triangle with legs $8$ (half the chord) and $6$ (the distance to the center). The hypotenuse is the radius: $\sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ cm.

solve.work: Perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord: half-chord 8, distance 6, r = sqrt(64+36) = 10.

questions.stem: In a circle of radius 5, a chord is 3 units from the center. How long is the chord?
questions.solution: The perpendicular from the center to the chord cuts it in half. In the right triangle with hypotenuse 5 (the radius) and one leg 3, the other leg is $\sqrt{25 - 9} = 4$. That is half the chord, so the chord is $2 \times 4 = 8$.

questions.stem: Point $P$ is 13 cm from the center of a circle whose radius is 5 cm. A tangent line from $P$ touches the circle at $T$. How long is $\overline{PT}$, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The radius to $T$ is perpendicular to the tangent, so the triangle formed by the center, $T$ and $P$ has a right angle at $T$. Its hypotenuse is 13 and one leg is 5, so $PT = \sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = \sqrt{144} = 12$ cm.

solve.work: OT is perpendicular to PT: PT = sqrt(13^2 - 5^2) = sqrt(144) = 12.

questions.stem: From point $P$, two tangent segments $\overline{PA}$ and $\overline{PB}$ are drawn to a circle, touching it at $A$ and $B$. If $PA = 3x + 2$ and $PB = 5x - 6$, what is $PA$?
questions.solution: Two tangent segments drawn to a circle from the same point are equal, so $3x + 2 = 5x - 6$. Then $8 = 2x$ and $x = 4$. So $PA = 3 \times 4 + 2 = 14$. (Check: $PB = 5 \times 4 - 6 = 14$.)

solve.work: Tangent segments from one point are equal: 3x+2 = 5x-6, x = 4, PA = 14 (PB = 14 too).

questions.stem: A circle has a diameter of $(3x - 4)$ cm and a radius of $(x + 3)$ cm. What is the diameter, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The diameter is twice the radius: $3x - 4 = 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6$, so $x = 10$. The diameter is $3(10) - 4 = 26$ cm. (The radius is 13 cm.)

questions.stem: Which of these could be the length of a chord of a circle with a radius of 5 cm?
questions.solution: The longest chord is a diameter, which is $2 \times 5 = 10$ cm here. A chord cannot be longer than 10 cm, so only 9.5 cm is possible.

solve.work: A chord is at most the diameter, 10 cm. Only 9.5 cm is at most 10.

questions.stem: Point $P$ is inside a circle of radius 9 cm, and it is 4 cm from the center. What is the greatest possible distance from $P$ to a point on the circle, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The farthest point on the circle is on the other side of the center, along the line from $P$ through the center. That distance is the 4 cm from $P$ to the center plus the 9 cm radius: $4 + 9 = 13$ cm.

solve.work: Farthest point is on the line through P and the center, on the far side: 9 + 4 = 13.

questions.stem: Circle $A$ has a circumference three times as large as the circumference of circle $B$. Circle $B$ has a radius of 5 cm. What is the radius of circle $A$, in centimeters?
questions.solution: Circumference is proportional to radius ($C = 2\pi r$), so tripling the circumference triples the radius: $3 \times 5 = 15$ cm.

solve.work: Circumference is proportional to radius: r_A = 3(5) = 15.

questions.stem: The diameter of a circle is doubled. What happens to its circumference?
questions.solution: The circumference is $\pi d$. If $d$ becomes $2d$, the circumference becomes $2\pi d$, which is twice as large.

solve.work: C = pi d, so doubling d doubles C.

questions.stem: A circular flower bed has a circumference of $20\pi$ meters. A path 1 meter wide goes all the way around it. The outer edge of the path has a circumference of $k\pi$ meters. What is $k$?
questions.solution: The flower bed has radius $20\pi \div 2\pi = 10$ m. The outer edge of the path has radius $10 + 1 = 11$ m, so its circumference is $2\pi \times 11 = 22\pi$ and $k = 22$.

solve.work: 2 pi r = 20pi gives r = 10; outer radius 11; outer circumference 22pi, k = 22.

questions.stem: A circle has an area of $100\pi$ square centimeters. What is its diameter, in centimeters?
questions.solution: $\pi r^2 = 100\pi$ gives $r = 10$, so the diameter is $2 \times 10 = 20$ cm. (10 is the radius.)

questions.stem: A circle has an area of $64\pi$ square centimeters. Its circumference is $k\pi$ centimeters. What is $k$?
questions.solution: $\pi r^2 = 64\pi$ gives $r = 8$. The circumference is $2\pi \times 8 = 16\pi$, so $k = 16$.

questions.stem: The radius of a circle is tripled. What happens to the area of the circle?
questions.solution: The area is $\pi r^2$. With radius $3r$ the area is $\pi (3r)^2 = 9\pi r^2$, which is 9 times as large.

solve.work: A = pi r^2; tripling r multiplies A by 9.

questions.stem: In a circle of radius 9 cm, an arc has a central angle of $80^\circ$. The length of the arc is $k\pi$ centimeters. What is $k$?
questions.solution: The circumference is $2\pi \times 9 = 18\pi$. The arc is $\frac{80}{360} = \frac{2}{9}$ of it: $18\pi \times \frac{2}{9} = 4\pi$, so $k = 4$.

questions.stem: A circle has a circumference of $24\pi$ cm. An arc of the circle is $7\pi$ cm long. What is the measure of its central angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: The arc is $\frac{7\pi}{24\pi} = \frac{7}{24}$ of the circumference, so its central angle is $\frac{7}{24} \times 360 = 105$ degrees.

questions.stem: A circle has a circumference of 36 cm. Points $A$ and $B$ are on the circle, and the minor arc $AB$ has a central angle of $110^\circ$. How long is the major arc $AB$, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The major arc has central angle $360 - 110 = 250$ degrees, which is $\frac{250}{360}$ of the circle: $36 \times \frac{250}{360} = 25$ cm.

questions.stem: A sector of a circle of radius 12 cm has a central angle of $150^\circ$. The area of the sector is $k\pi$ square centimeters. What is $k$?
questions.solution: The circle has area $\pi \times 12^2 = 144\pi$. The sector is $\frac{150}{360} = \frac{5}{12}$ of it: $144\pi \times \frac{5}{12} = 60\pi$, so $k = 60$.

questions.stem: A circle has an area of $84\pi$ square centimeters. A sector of the circle has an area of $14\pi$ square centimeters. What is the measure of its central angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: The sector is $\frac{14\pi}{84\pi} = \frac{1}{6}$ of the circle, so its central angle is $\frac{1}{6} \times 360 = 60$ degrees.

questions.stem: A sector of a circle with radius 5 cm has an arc length of $4\pi$ cm. The area of the sector is $k\pi$ square centimeters. What is $k$?
questions.solution: The whole circumference is $2\pi \times 5 = 10\pi$, so the sector is $\frac{4\pi}{10\pi} = \frac{2}{5}$ of the circle. The circle's area is $25\pi$, so the sector's area is $\frac{2}{5} \times 25\pi = 10\pi$ and $k = 10$.

questions.stem: A chord 24 cm long is drawn in a circle of radius 13 cm. How far is the chord from the center of the circle, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The perpendicular from the center bisects the chord, forming a right triangle with legs 12 (half the chord) and $d$ (the distance), and hypotenuse 13 (the radius). So $d^2 = 13^2 - 12^2 = 25$ and $d = 5$ cm.

questions.stem: A chord of a circle with radius 17 is 8 units from the center. How long is the chord?
questions.solution: Half the chord is the leg of a right triangle with the other leg 8 and hypotenuse 17: $\sqrt{17^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{225} = 15$. The whole chord is $2 \times 15 = 30$.

questions.stem: Chords $AB$ and $CD$ of the same circle are equal in length. Chord $AB$ is 7 cm from the center of the circle. How far is chord $CD$ from the center, in centimeters?
questions.solution: Equal chords of one circle make congruent right triangles with the radius and the perpendicular from the center, so they are the same distance from the center. $CD$ is also 7 cm from the center.

solve.work: Equal chords are equidistant from the center: 7.

questions.stem: The line $PT$ is tangent at $T$ to a circle with center $O$. If $OT = 9$ cm and $PT = 12$ cm, how long is $\overline{OP}$, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The radius $OT$ is perpendicular to the tangent $PT$, so triangle $OTP$ has a right angle at $T$. Then $OP^2 = 9^2 + 12^2 = 225$ and $OP = 15$ cm.

solve.work: OT is perpendicular to PT: OP = sqrt(81 + 144) = 15.

questions.stem: The line $PT$ is tangent at $T$ to a circle with center $O$, and $\angle TOP = 40^\circ$. What is the measure of $\angle OPT$, in degrees?
questions.solution: The radius $OT$ is perpendicular to the tangent, so $\angle OTP = 90^\circ$. The angles of triangle $OTP$ add to $180^\circ$: $\angle OPT = 180 - 90 - 40 = 50^\circ$.

questions.stem: The line $PT$ is tangent at $T$ to a circle with center $O$ and radius 3 cm. The distance $OP$ is 5 cm. What is the perimeter of triangle $OTP$, in centimeters?
questions.solution: Triangle $OTP$ has a right angle at $T$, with $OT = 3$ and $OP = 5$. So $PT = \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = 4$. The perimeter is $3 + 4 + 5 = 12$ cm.

questions.stem: The shortest distance from the center of a circle to a line is 5 cm, and the circle has a radius of 8 cm. How many points do the line and the circle have in common?
questions.solution: The line is closer to the center (5 cm) than the radius (8 cm), so it cuts through the circle and meets it in 2 points. (It would touch at only one point if its distance were exactly 8 cm.)

solve.work: Distance 5 < radius 8, so the line is a secant: 2 points.

questions.stem: A half-circle region has a straight edge that is a diameter of 12 cm. What is the area of the half-circle region, in square centimeters?
questions.solution: The radius is $12 \div 2 = 6$ cm. The full circle has area $\pi \times 6^2 = 36\pi$, and half of it is $18\pi$ square centimeters.

questions.stem: A wheel has a radius of 20 cm. It rolls along a straight path without slipping and makes exactly 5 full turns. The distance it rolls is $k\pi$ centimeters. What is $k$?
questions.solution: In one full turn the wheel rolls a distance equal to its circumference: $2\pi \times 20 = 40\pi$ cm. In 5 turns it rolls $5 \times 40\pi = 200\pi$ cm, so $k = 200$.

questions.stem: Two circles have the same center. The larger has radius 10 and the smaller has radius 6. What is the area of the ring between the two circles?
questions.solution: The ring is the large disk with the small disk removed: $\pi \times 10^2 - \pi \times 6^2 = 100\pi - 36\pi = 64\pi$. (Subtracting the radii first, which gives $16\pi$, does not work because area depends on the square of the radius.)

questions.stem: A circle has radius 12. An arc of the circle has length $5\pi$. What is the measure of the arc's central angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: The whole circumference is $2\pi \times 12 = 24\pi$. The arc is $\frac{5\pi}{24\pi} = \frac{5}{24}$ of the circle, so its central angle is $\frac{5}{24} \times 360^\circ = 75^\circ$.

questions.stem: A sector of a circle of radius 8 has a central angle of $90^\circ$. What is the perimeter of the sector, which is the curved edge plus the two straight edges?
questions.solution: The curved edge is $\frac{90}{360} = \frac{1}{4}$ of the circumference $2\pi \times 8 = 16\pi$, which is $4\pi$. The two straight edges are radii, $8 + 8 = 16$. The perimeter is $16 + 4\pi$.

questions.stem: A sector of a circle has area $12\pi$ and a central angle of $120^\circ$. What is the radius of the circle?
questions.solution: The sector is $\frac{120}{360} = \frac{1}{3}$ of the circle, so the whole circle has area $3 \times 12\pi = 36\pi$. From $\pi r^2 = 36\pi$ we get $r^2 = 36$, so $r = 6$.

questions.stem: Two parallel chords of lengths 12 and 16 are drawn in a circle of radius 10, on opposite sides of the center. How far apart are the two chords?
questions.solution: The center is $\sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = 8$ from the chord of length 12 (half the chord is 6), and $\sqrt{10^2 - 8^2} = 6$ from the chord of length 16 (half is 8). On opposite sides of the center, the chords are $8 + 6 = 14$ apart. (On the same side they would be $8 - 6 = 2$ apart.)

solve.work: Chord 12: distance sqrt(100-36) = 8. Chord 16: distance sqrt(100-64) = 6. Opposite sides: 8 + 6 = 14.

questions.stem: A chord of a circle is 16 cm long. The segment from the midpoint of the chord to the midpoint of the shorter arc cut off by the chord is 4 cm long. What is the radius of the circle, in centimeters?
questions.solution: Let the radius be $r$. The center lies on the perpendicular bisector of the chord, $r - 4$ from the chord on the other side from the shorter arc. Half the chord is 8, so $8^2 + (r - 4)^2 = r^2$. That gives $64 + r^2 - 8r + 16 = r^2$, so $80 = 8r$ and $r = 10$.

solve.work: The line through the chord's midpoint and the arc's midpoint passes through the centre. Centre to chord distance = r - 4, half chord 8: (r-4)^2 + 64 = r^2, -8r + 80 = 0, r = 10.

questions.stem: Two circles are tangent to each other on the outside, one with radius 4 and one with radius 9. A line touches the small circle at $A$ and the large circle at $B$, with both circles on the same side of the line. What is $AB$?
questions.solution: The centers are $4 + 9 = 13$ apart. Draw the radii to $A$ and $B$; both are perpendicular to the line. From the center of the small circle draw a segment parallel to $\overline{AB}$ to the large circle's radius. This makes a right triangle with hypotenuse 13 and one leg $9 - 4 = 5$. The other leg equals $AB$: $\sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = \sqrt{144} = 12$.

solve.work: Centres 4 + 9 = 13 apart. Common external tangent: AB = sqrt(13^2 - (9-4)^2) = sqrt(144) = 12.

questions.stem: The center of a circle is $O$ and its radius is 8. Point $P$ is 17 from $O$. Tangent segments $\overline{PA}$ and $\overline{PB}$ touch the circle at $A$ and $B$. What is the perimeter of quadrilateral $OAPB$?
questions.solution: The radii $\overline{OA}$ and $\overline{OB}$ are perpendicular to the tangents, so triangle $OAP$ has a right angle at $A$, with hypotenuse 17 and leg 8. Then $PA = \sqrt{17^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{225} = 15$, and $PB = 15$ too. The perimeter is $8 + 15 + 15 + 8 = 46$.

questions.stem: Three identical circles are placed in a row, each touching the next. A rectangle just encloses all three: it touches each circle at the top and bottom, and the two end circles at the ends. The perimeter of the rectangle is 64 cm. What is the radius of each circle, in centimeters?
questions.solution: If the radius is $r$, each circle is $2r$ wide, so the rectangle is $3 \times 2r = 6r$ long and $2r$ tall. Its perimeter is $2(6r + 2r) = 16r$. From $16r = 64$ we get $r = 4$ cm.

solve.work: Rectangle is 6r long and 2r tall: perimeter 2(6r + 2r) = 16r = 64, r = 4.

questions.stem: Four identical circles sit in a row, each touching the next, with their centers on one straight line. The row, from the leftmost point of the first circle to the rightmost point of the last, is 56 cm long. What is the radius of each circle, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The row is made of 4 diameters laid end to end, so one diameter is $56 \div 4 = 14$ cm. The radius is $14 \div 2 = 7$ cm.

questions.stem: Point $O$ is the center of a circle, and $A$ and $B$ are points on the circle with $AB = 8$ cm. Triangle $OAB$ has a perimeter of 30 cm. What is the radius of the circle, in centimeters?
questions.solution: $OA$ and $OB$ are both radii, so each is $r$. The perimeter is $r + r + 8 = 30$, so $2r = 22$ and $r = 11$ cm.

questions.stem: Circle $X$ has a diameter of 10 cm. Circle $Y$ has a radius of 5 cm. Circle $Z$ has a circumference of $10\pi$ cm. Which statement is true?
choices: All three circles have the same radius.
questions.answer: All three circles have the same radius.
questions.solution: Circle $X$ has radius $10 \div 2 = 5$ cm. Circle $Y$ has radius 5 cm. Circle $Z$ has radius $10\pi \div 2\pi = 5$ cm. All three radii are equal.

solve.answer: All three circles have the same radius.
solve.work: X: r = 5; Y: r = 5; Z: 2 pi r = 10pi, r = 5. All equal.

questions.stem: A wheel of radius 25 cm rolls along a straight road without slipping and covers a distance of $1000\pi$ cm. How many full turns does the wheel make?
questions.solution: In one turn the wheel rolls its circumference, $2\pi \times 25 = 50\pi$ cm. The number of turns is $1000\pi \div 50\pi = 20$.

questions.stem: A wire $30\pi$ cm long is bent into two circles, using all of the wire. The radius of the larger circle is twice the radius of the smaller circle. What is the radius of the larger circle, in centimeters?
questions.solution: Let the smaller radius be $r$. The circumferences are $2\pi r$ and $2\pi (2r) = 4\pi r$, and together they are $6\pi r = 30\pi$. So $r = 5$ and the larger radius is $2r = 10$ cm.

solve.work: 2 pi r + 2 pi (2r) = 6 pi r = 30pi, r = 5; larger radius 10.

questions.stem: Two round gears touch at their edges and turn without slipping, so the same length of edge passes the touching point on each. The larger gear has a radius of 12 cm and the smaller gear has a radius of 8 cm. When the larger gear makes 2 full turns, how many turns does the smaller gear make?
questions.solution: Two turns of the larger gear pass $2 \times 2\pi \times 12 = 48\pi$ cm of edge. One turn of the smaller gear is $2\pi \times 8 = 16\pi$ cm, so it makes $48\pi \div 16\pi = 3$ turns.

solve.work: Larger gear: 2 turns x 24pi = 48pi of edge. Smaller: 16pi per turn; 48pi/16pi = 3.

questions.stem: A circular garden has a radius of 6 meters. A path of the same width goes all the way around it. The garden and the path together have an area of $100\pi$ square meters. How wide is the path, in meters?
questions.solution: The garden and path together form a circle with area $100\pi$, so its radius is 10 m. The path's width is the difference of the radii: $10 - 6 = 4$ m.

questions.stem: The area of a circle in square units is equal to its circumference in units. What is the radius of the circle?
questions.solution: Set $\pi r^2 = 2\pi r$. Dividing both sides by $\pi r$ (which is not 0) gives $r = 2$.

questions.stem: Two circles have radii 3 and 4. A third circle has an area equal to the sum of the areas of the first two. What is the radius of the third circle?
questions.solution: The areas are $9\pi$ and $16\pi$, with sum $25\pi$. So $\pi r^2 = 25\pi$ and $r = 5$. (Radii do not simply add, and 25 is the radius squared.)

questions.stem: A circle of radius 10 cm has a sector with a central angle of $72^\circ$ cut away. What is the area of the part of the circle that is left, in square centimeters?
questions.solution: The circle has area $100\pi$. The cut-away sector is $\frac{72}{360} = \frac{1}{5}$ of it, $20\pi$. What is left is $100\pi - 20\pi = 80\pi$ square centimeters.

questions.stem: A sector of a circle with radius 6 cm has a perimeter of $12 + 5\pi$ cm (the curved edge plus the two straight edges). What is the measure of its central angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: The two straight edges are radii and add to 12 cm, so the curved edge is $5\pi$ cm. The whole circumference is $12\pi$, so the arc is $\frac{5\pi}{12\pi} = \frac{5}{12}$ of the circle: $\frac{5}{12} \times 360 = 150$ degrees.

questions.stem: Circle $A$ has radius 8 and an arc with a central angle of $90^\circ$. Circle $B$ has radius 12 and an arc of the same length as circle $A$'s arc. What is the central angle of the arc of circle $B$, in degrees?
questions.solution: The arc on circle $A$ is $\frac{90}{360} \times 2\pi \times 8 = 4\pi$. On circle $B$ the same length $4\pi$ is $\frac{4\pi}{24\pi} = \frac{1}{6}$ of the circumference, so the angle is $\frac{1}{6} \times 360 = 60$ degrees.

questions.stem: The minute hand of a clock is 15 cm long and turns through a full circle in 60 minutes. In 20 minutes, the tip of the hand travels a distance of $k\pi$ centimeters along a circular arc. What is $k$?
questions.solution: In 20 minutes the hand turns $\frac{20}{60} = \frac{1}{3}$ of a full circle. The tip's circle has circumference $2\pi \times 15 = 30\pi$, so the tip travels $30\pi \div 3 = 10\pi$ and $k = 10$.

questions.stem: A sector of a circle has a radius of 6 cm and an arc length of $4\pi$ cm. The area of the sector is $k\pi$ square centimeters. What is $k$?
questions.solution: The circumference is $12\pi$, so the sector is $\frac{4\pi}{12\pi} = \frac{1}{3}$ of the circle. The circle's area is $36\pi$, so the sector's area is $36\pi \div 3 = 12\pi$ and $k = 12$.

questions.stem: Two diameters of a circle of radius 8 cross at an angle of $60^\circ$. They cut the circle into four sectors: two with central angle $60^\circ$ and two with central angle $120^\circ$. What is the combined area of the two sectors with central angle $60^\circ$, in square centimeters?
questions.solution: The circle has area $64\pi$. Each $60^\circ$ sector is $\frac{1}{6}$ of it, $\frac{64\pi}{6}$, so the two together are $\frac{64\pi}{3}$ square centimeters.

questions.stem: Sector $A$ has a radius of 6 cm and a central angle of $60^\circ$. Sector $B$ has a radius of 4 cm and the same area as sector $A$. What is the central angle of sector $B$, in degrees?
questions.solution: Sector $A$ has area $\frac{60}{360} \times 36\pi = 6\pi$. Sector $B$ has area $\frac{x}{360} \times 16\pi$, and setting this equal to $6\pi$ gives $x = \frac{6 \times 360}{16} = 135$ degrees.

questions.stem: A circle has a radius of 10. Point $P$ is inside the circle, 6 units from the center $O$. Of all the chords that pass through $P$, how long is the shortest one?
questions.solution: The shortest chord through $P$ is the one perpendicular to $OP$, since it is the farthest from the center. Half of it is the leg of a right triangle with hypotenuse 10 and other leg 6, so half is $\sqrt{100 - 36} = 8$. The chord is $16$.

solve.work: Shortest chord through P is perpendicular to OP: 2 sqrt(100 - 36) = 16.

questions.stem: Two circles have the same center, with radii 5 and 13. A chord of the larger circle is tangent to the smaller circle. How long is the chord?
questions.solution: The chord touches the smaller circle at a point whose radius (5) is perpendicular to the chord, so that radius cuts the chord in half. Half the chord is $\sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = 12$, so the chord is $24$.

solve.work: Chord is at distance 5 from center: 2 sqrt(169 - 25) = 2(12) = 24.

questions.stem: In a circle of radius 17, two parallel chords of lengths 16 and 30 are on the same side of the center. How far apart are the two chords?
questions.solution: The chord of length 16 is $\sqrt{17^2 - 8^2} = 15$ from the center, and the chord of length 30 is $\sqrt{17^2 - 15^2} = 8$ from the center. On the same side of the center they are $15 - 8 = 7$ apart. (On opposite sides it would be 23.)

solve.work: Distances: chord 16: sqrt(289 - 64) = 15; chord 30: sqrt(289 - 225) = 8. Same side: 15 - 8 = 7.

questions.stem: A right triangle has legs 6 and 8 and hypotenuse 10. A circle inside the triangle touches all three sides. What is the radius of the circle?
questions.solution: Let the radius be $r$. The tangent segments from the right-angle vertex to the circle are each $r$, so the rest of each leg is $6 - r$ and $8 - r$. Tangent segments from one point are equal, so the hypotenuse is $(6 - r) + (8 - r) = 10$. Then $14 - 2r = 10$ and $r = 2$.

solve.work: Inradius of right triangle = (a + b - c)/2 = (6 + 8 - 10)/2 = 2 (also area 24 / semiperimeter 12).

questions.stem: A quadrilateral $ABCD$ has a circle inside it that touches all four sides. If $AB = 7$, $BC = 8$ and $CD = 9$, what is $DA$?
questions.solution: Let the tangent lengths from $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ be $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$. Then $AB = a + b$, $BC = b + c$, $CD = c + d$, $DA = d + a$. So $AB + CD = BC + DA$, giving $DA = 7 + 9 - 8 = 8$.

solve.work: Tangential quadrilateral (Pitot): AB + CD = BC + DA, 7 + 9 = 8 + DA, DA = 8.

questions.stem: The line $PT$ is tangent at $T$ to a circle with center $O$ and radius 8. The length $PT$ is 15. The segment $OP$ crosses the circle at the point $Q$. What is $PQ$?
questions.solution: Triangle $OTP$ has a right angle at $T$, so $OP = \sqrt{8^2 + 15^2} = 17$. $OQ$ is a radius, 8, so $PQ = 17 - 8 = 9$.

solve.work: OP = sqrt(64 + 225) = 17; Q is on circle between O and P, so PQ = 17 - 8 = 9.

questions.stem: The line $PT$ is tangent at $T$ to a circle with center $O$. The length $PT$ is 24 and $OP$ is 25. What is the radius of the circle?
questions.solution: Triangle $OTP$ has a right angle at $T$ (a radius meets a tangent at $90^\circ$). So $OT^2 = OP^2 - PT^2 = 625 - 576 = 49$ and the radius $OT$ is 7.

solve.work: OT perpendicular to PT: r = sqrt(625 - 576) = 7.

questions.stem: Points A and B lie on a circle, and the minor arc AB measures $100^\circ$. What is the measure, in degrees, of the major arc AB?
questions.solution: The minor arc and the major arc together make the whole circle, which is $360^\circ$. So the major arc is $360 - 100 = 260$ degrees.

questions.stem: O is the center of a circle, and A and B are points on the circle with $\angle AOB = 72^\circ$. What is the measure, in degrees, of the minor arc AB?
questions.solution: A central angle has the same measure as the arc it cuts off, so arc AB is $72^\circ$. (36 would be the inscribed angle on that arc, and 144 is double the arc.)

solve.work: A minor arc equals its central angle: 72.

questions.stem: An inscribed angle in a circle cuts off an arc of $80^\circ$. What is the measure, in degrees, of the inscribed angle?
questions.solution: An inscribed angle is half of the arc it cuts off: $80 \div 2 = 40$ degrees.

questions.stem: Points A, B and C lie on a circle, and $\angle ACB = 35^\circ$. What is the measure, in degrees, of the arc AB that does not contain C?
questions.solution: The arc is twice the inscribed angle: $2 \times 35 = 70$ degrees. (35 forgets to double, 17.5 halves instead, and 145 is $180 - 35$.)

questions.skill: Angle in a semicircle and angles on the same arc
questions.stem: Two inscribed angles of a circle cut off the same arc. One of them measures $28^\circ$. What is the measure, in degrees, of the other?
questions.solution: Each inscribed angle is half of the same arc, so the two angles are equal. The other angle is also $28^\circ$.

solve.work: Inscribed angles on the same arc are equal: 28.

questions.skill: Angle in a semicircle and angles on the same arc
questions.stem: Segment AB is a diameter of a circle, and C is another point on the circle. What is the measure, in degrees, of $\angle ACB$?
questions.solution: The diameter cuts off a semicircle of $180^\circ$. The inscribed angle $\angle ACB$ is half of that arc, so it measures $90^\circ$: an angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

questions.stem: Quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed in a circle, which means all four of its vertices are on the circle. If $\angle A = 100^\circ$, what is the measure, in degrees, of $\angle C$, the angle opposite A?
questions.solution: Opposite angles of an inscribed quadrilateral add up to $180^\circ$. So $\angle C = 180 - 100 = 80$ degrees.

solve.work: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180: 180 - 100 = 80.

questions.skill: Angles formed by two chords inside a circle
questions.stem: Chords AB and CD of a circle cross at a point P inside the circle. The angle $\angle APC$ cuts off arc AC, and its vertical angle $\angle BPD$ cuts off arc BD. Arc AC measures $50^\circ$ and arc BD measures $90^\circ$. What is the measure of $\angle APC$ in degrees?
questions.solution: The angle formed by two chords is half the sum of the two arcs cut off by the angle and its vertical angle: $\frac{1}{2}(50 + 90) = 70$ degrees.

solve.work: Angle between chords = half the sum of the intercepted arcs: (50 + 90)/2 = 70.

questions.stem: Line PT is tangent at the point T to a circle with center O, and $\angle OPT = 35^\circ$. What is the measure, in degrees, of $\angle POT$?
questions.solution: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency, so $\angle OTP = 90^\circ$. The angles of triangle OPT add up to $180^\circ$, so $\angle POT = 180 - 90 - 35 = 55$ degrees.

solve.work: Radius OT is perpendicular to the tangent, so angle OTP = 90; angle POT = 180 - 90 - 35 = 55.

questions.skill: Angles formed by secants and tangents outside a circle
questions.stem: Two secants meet at a point P outside a circle. Between them they cut off a far arc of $100^\circ$ and a near arc of $40^\circ$. What is the measure, in degrees, of the angle at P between the secants?
questions.solution: An angle formed outside a circle is half the difference of the arcs it cuts off: $\frac{1}{2}(100 - 40) = 30$ degrees. (70 is half the sum, 140 is the sum, and 60 is the difference.)

solve.work: Angle between secants outside = half the difference of arcs: (100 - 40)/2 = 30.

questions.stem: $O$ is the center of a circle, and $A$ and $B$ are points on the circle with $\angle AOB = 115^\circ$ (the angle that opens toward the minor arc). What is the measure of the minor arc $AB$, in degrees?
questions.solution: A central angle has the same measure as the arc it cuts off, so the minor arc $AB$ measures $115^\circ$.

solve.work: A minor arc equals its central angle: 115.

questions.stem: Three points on a circle divide it into three arcs of equal measure. What is the measure of each arc, in degrees?
questions.solution: The arcs of a full circle add to $360^\circ$, so each is $360 \div 3 = 120^\circ$.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$ and $C$ divide a circle into three arcs: $AB$, $BC$ and $CA$. Arc $AB$ measures $100^\circ$ and arc $BC$ measures $120^\circ$. What is the measure of arc $CA$, in degrees?
questions.solution: The three arcs make a full circle, $360^\circ$. So arc $CA = 360 - 100 - 120 = 140^\circ$.

questions.stem: The minor arc $AB$ of a circle measures $60^\circ$. What fraction of the whole circle is the major arc $AB$?
questions.solution: The major arc measures $360 - 60 = 300$ degrees, and $\frac{300}{360} = \frac{5}{6}$ of the circle.

questions.stem: An inscribed angle in a circle measures $62^\circ$. What is the measure of the arc it cuts off, in degrees?
questions.solution: An inscribed angle is half the arc it cuts off, so the arc is $2 \times 62 = 124^\circ$.

questions.stem: An inscribed angle cuts off an arc of $150^\circ$. What is the measure of the inscribed angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: An inscribed angle is half of the arc it cuts off: $150 \div 2 = 75^\circ$.

questions.stem: In a circle with center $O$, the central angle $\angle AOB$ measures $90^\circ$. An inscribed angle $\angle ACB$ cuts off the same minor arc $AB$. What is the measure of $\angle ACB$, in degrees?
questions.solution: The central angle and the inscribed angle cut off the same arc, which measures $90^\circ$. The inscribed angle is half of it: $45^\circ$.

solve.work: Minor arc AB = 90; inscribed angle on it = 45.

questions.stem: Points $P$, $Q$ and $R$ lie on a circle, and $\angle PRQ = 90^\circ$. What is the measure of the arc $PQ$ that does not contain $R$, in degrees?
questions.solution: The arc is twice the inscribed angle: $2 \times 90 = 180^\circ$. (So $PQ$ is a diameter.)

solve.work: Inscribed angle 90 cuts off arc 180 (PQ is a diameter).

questions.skill: Angle in a semicircle and angles on the same arc
questions.stem: Triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle, and $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter. Which angle of the triangle must be a right angle?
choices: None of them has to be a right angle
questions.solution: An angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle. $\angle C$ opens onto the diameter $AB$, which cuts off a semicircle of $180^\circ$, so $\angle C = 90^\circ$.

solve.work: Angle inscribed in a semicircle is right; the angle opposite diameter AB is at C.

questions.skill: Angle in a semicircle and angles on the same arc
questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter of a circle. What is the measure, in degrees, of the semicircle arc $AB$?
questions.solution: A diameter splits a circle into two equal arcs, each half of $360^\circ$, so each measures $180^\circ$.

questions.skill: Angle in a semicircle and angles on the same arc
questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on a circle, with $C$ and $D$ on the same side of line $AB$. If $\angle ACB = 55^\circ$, what is the measure of $\angle ADB$, in degrees?
questions.solution: Both angles are inscribed angles that cut off the same arc $AB$, so they are equal: $\angle ADB = 55^\circ$.

solve.work: Inscribed angles on the same arc AB from the same side are equal: 55.

questions.stem: Quadrilateral $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle, and $\angle B = 85^\circ$. What is the measure of $\angle D$, the angle opposite $B$, in degrees?
questions.solution: Opposite angles of an inscribed quadrilateral add to $180^\circ$, so $\angle D = 180 - 85 = 95^\circ$.

solve.work: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary: 180 - 85 = 95.

questions.stem: Quadrilateral $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle. Which pair of its angles must add up to $180^\circ$?
choices: Two angles that share a side
questions.solution: In an inscribed quadrilateral, each pair of opposite angles is supplementary: they add to $180^\circ$. Angles that share a side need not.

solve.work: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180.

questions.stem: Quadrilateral $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle, and $\angle A = \angle C$. What is the measure of $\angle A$, in degrees?
questions.solution: $\angle A$ and $\angle C$ are opposite angles, so $\angle A + \angle C = 180^\circ$. If they are equal, each is $180 \div 2 = 90^\circ$.

solve.work: A + C = 180 and A = C, so A = 90.

questions.skill: Angles formed by two chords inside a circle
questions.stem: Two chords cross inside a circle. The angle they form cuts off an arc of $30^\circ$, and its vertical angle cuts off an arc of $90^\circ$. What is the measure of the angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: An angle formed by two chords inside a circle is half the sum of the arcs it and its vertical angle cut off: $\frac{30 + 90}{2} = 60^\circ$.

questions.skill: Angles formed by two chords inside a circle
questions.stem: Chords $AC$ and $BD$ cross at a point $E$ inside a circle. The angle $\angle AEB$ cuts off arc $AB$, which measures $70^\circ$, and its vertical angle $\angle CED$ cuts off arc $CD$, which measures $110^\circ$. What is the measure of $\angle AEB$, in degrees?
questions.solution: The angle is half the sum of the two arcs: $\frac{70 + 110}{2} = 90^\circ$.

questions.skill: Angles formed by two chords inside a circle
questions.stem: Two chords cross inside a circle. How is the measure of one of the angles they form found from the arcs?
choices: Half the difference of those two arcs
The sum of those two arcs
Half the sum of the arc it cuts off and the arc its vertical angle cuts off
The difference of those two arcs
questions.answer: Half the sum of the arc it cuts off and the arc its vertical angle cuts off
questions.solution: For two chords meeting inside a circle, the angle equals half the sum of the arc it cuts off and the arc cut off by its vertical angle. (Half the difference is the rule for an angle outside the circle.)

solve.answer: Half the sum of the arc it cuts off and the arc its vertical angle cuts off
solve.issues: Minor wording: three options refer to "those two arcs", which has no antecedent in the stem. The correct option is still clear.
solve.work: Chord-chord angle = half the sum of the intercepted arc and the vertical angle's arc.

questions.stem: A line is tangent to a circle at the point $T$, and $\overline{TB}$ is a chord. The arc $TB$ inside the angle between the tangent and the chord measures $70^\circ$. What is the measure of the angle between the tangent and the chord, in degrees?
questions.solution: The angle between a tangent and a chord is half the arc it cuts off: $70 \div 2 = 35^\circ$.

questions.stem: A line is tangent to a circle at $T$, and $\overline{TB}$ is a chord. How is the angle between the tangent and the chord related to the arc it cuts off?
choices: The angle is equal to the arc.
The angle is twice the arc.
The angle and the arc add to $180^\circ$.
The angle is half the arc.
questions.answer: The angle is half the arc.
questions.solution: A tangent-chord angle is like an inscribed angle: its measure is half of the arc it cuts off.

solve.answer: The angle is half the arc.
solve.work: Tangent-chord angle is half the intercepted arc.

questions.stem: A line is tangent to a circle at the point $T$, and $\overline{TB}$ is a chord. The angle between the tangent and the chord measures $48^\circ$. What is the measure of the arc $TB$ inside that angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: The arc is twice the tangent-chord angle: $2 \times 48 = 96^\circ$.

questions.skill: Angles formed by secants and tangents outside a circle
questions.stem: Two secants meet at a point outside a circle. How is the angle between them found from the two arcs they cut off?
choices: Half the difference of the far arc and the near arc
Half the sum of the far arc and the near arc
The difference of the far arc and the near arc
The sum of the far arc and the near arc
questions.answer: Half the difference of the far arc and the near arc
questions.solution: An angle formed outside a circle by two secants is half the difference of the arcs it cuts off: the far arc minus the near arc, divided by 2.

solve.answer: Half the difference of the far arc and the near arc
solve.work: Angle formed outside = half the difference of far and near arcs.

questions.skill: Angles formed by secants and tangents outside a circle
questions.stem: Two tangents from a point $P$ outside a circle touch it at $A$ and $B$. They cut off a minor arc $AB$ of $120^\circ$ and a major arc $AB$ of $240^\circ$. What is the measure of $\angle APB$, in degrees?
questions.solution: The angle is half the difference of the arcs: $\frac{240 - 120}{2} = 60^\circ$.

questions.skill: Angles formed by secants and tangents outside a circle
questions.stem: Two secants meet at a point $P$ outside a circle. Between them they cut off a far arc of $150^\circ$ and a near arc of $50^\circ$. What is the measure of the angle at $P$, in degrees?
questions.solution: The angle is half the difference of the far and near arcs: $\frac{150 - 50}{2} = 50^\circ$.

questions.stem: Points are placed around a circle so that they split it into equal arcs, and the central angle between neighboring points is $24^\circ$. How many points are there?
questions.solution: The central angles around the circle add up to $360^\circ$. The number of equal arcs is $360 \div 24 = 15$, and there are as many points as arcs, so 15.

questions.stem: Points P, Q and R lie on a circle. The inscribed angle $\angle PRQ$ measures $(2x+10)^\circ$, and the arc PQ that does not contain R measures $(5x+10)^\circ$. What is the measure of $\angle PRQ$ in degrees?
questions.solution: The inscribed angle is half its arc: $2x + 10 = \frac{5x + 10}{2}$. Then $4x + 20 = 5x + 10$, so $x = 10$. The angle is $2(10) + 10 = 30$ degrees. (Check: the arc is $5(10) + 10 = 60$, and half of 60 is 30.)

questions.stem: O is the center of a circle, and A, B and C are points on it. The central angle $\angle AOB$ and the inscribed angle $\angle ACB$ cut off the same minor arc AB, and $\angle AOB$ is $25^\circ$ larger than $\angle ACB$. What is the measure, in degrees, of arc AB?
questions.solution: The central angle is twice the inscribed angle, so it is larger by exactly the inscribed angle. So $\angle ACB = 25^\circ$ and $\angle AOB = 50^\circ$. Arc AB equals the central angle, $50^\circ$. (25 is the inscribed angle, and 75 is the sum of the two angles.)

solve.work: AOB = arc, ACB = arc/2; arc - arc/2 = 25 -> arc = 50.

questions.skill: Angle in a semicircle and angles on the same arc
questions.stem: Segment AB is a diameter of a circle, and C is a point on the circle other than A and B. If $\angle CAB = 38^\circ$, what is the measure of $\angle ABC$ in degrees?
questions.solution: An angle in a semicircle is a right angle, so $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$. The angles of triangle ABC add up to $180^\circ$, so $\angle ABC = 180 - 90 - 38 = 52$ degrees.

questions.stem: Quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed in a circle. Its angle $\angle A$ measures $(2x)^\circ$ and the opposite angle $\angle C$ measures $(x + 30)^\circ$. What is the measure, in degrees, of $\angle A$?
questions.solution: Opposite angles of an inscribed quadrilateral add up to $180^\circ$: $2x + (x + 30) = 180$, so $3x = 150$ and $x = 50$. Then $\angle A = 2(50) = 100$ degrees. (50 is $x$, 80 is $\angle C$, and 60 comes from wrongly setting the two angles equal.)

questions.skill: Angles formed by two chords inside a circle
questions.stem: Two chords cross inside a circle and form an angle of $70^\circ$. This angle cuts off an arc of $50^\circ$. What is the measure, in degrees, of the arc cut off by its vertical angle?
questions.solution: The angle is half the sum of the two arcs, so the two arcs add up to $2 \times 70 = 140$ degrees. The other arc is $140 - 50 = 90$ degrees. (20 is $70 - 50$, and 120 is $70 + 50$.)

questions.skill: Angles formed by two chords inside a circle
questions.stem: Quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed in a circle, and its diagonals AC and BD cross at E. Arc AB measures $84^\circ$ and arc CD measures $56^\circ$ (each is the arc that does not contain the other two vertices). What is the measure, in degrees, of $\angle AEB$?
questions.solution: The angle $\angle AEB$ cuts off arc AB, and its vertical angle $\angle CED$ cuts off arc CD. The angle is half the sum of the two arcs: $\frac{1}{2}(84 + 56) = 70$ degrees. (28 is half the difference, 140 is the sum, and 35 halves twice.)

solve.work: Angle AEB intercepts arc AB and its vertical angle CED intercepts arc CD: (84 + 56)/2 = 70.

questions.stem: A line is tangent to a circle at the point T, and TB is a chord of the circle. The angle between the tangent line and the chord TB is $40^\circ$. What is the measure, in degrees, of the arc TB that lies inside this angle?
questions.solution: An angle formed by a tangent and a chord is half of the arc it cuts off. So the arc is $2 \times 40 = 80$ degrees.

solve.work: Tangent-chord angle = half the intercepted arc, so arc = 2*40 = 80.

questions.skill: Angles formed by secants and tangents outside a circle
questions.stem: Two secants meet at a point P outside a circle. The angle at P measures $20^\circ$, and the far arc cut off between the secants measures $110^\circ$. What is the measure, in degrees, of the near arc?
questions.solution: The angle is half the difference of the arcs: $20 = \frac{1}{2}(110 - n)$, where $n$ is the near arc. Then $110 - n = 40$, so $n = 70$ degrees.

questions.skill: Angles formed by secants and tangents outside a circle
questions.stem: From a point P outside a circle, two tangents touch the circle at A and B. The minor arc AB measures $110^\circ$. What is the measure, in degrees, of $\angle APB$?
questions.solution: The major arc AB is $360 - 110 = 250$ degrees. The angle at P is half the difference of the arcs: $\frac{1}{2}(250 - 110) = 70$ degrees. (Another way: the angles of quadrilateral PAOB add up to $360^\circ$, with two right angles and a $110^\circ$ angle at O, leaving $70^\circ$ at P.)

questions.stem: In a circle with center $O$, the minor arc $AB$ measures $(3x + 20)^\circ$ and the central angle $\angle AOB$ measures $(5x - 10)^\circ$. What is the measure of arc $AB$, in degrees?
questions.solution: A central angle equals its arc, so $3x + 20 = 5x - 10$, giving $x = 15$. The arc measures $3(15) + 20 = 65^\circ$.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ and $E$ lie in that order on a circle. Arcs $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ and $DE$ measure $50^\circ$, $70^\circ$, $90^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. What is the measure of arc $EA$, in degrees?
questions.solution: The five arcs add to $360^\circ$. The four given arcs total $50 + 70 + 90 + 60 = 270$, so arc $EA = 360 - 270 = 90^\circ$.

questions.stem: A regular octagon $ABCDEFGH$ is inscribed in a circle. What is the measure, in degrees, of arc $AC$ that contains $B$?
questions.solution: The 8 vertices split the circle into 8 equal arcs of $360 \div 8 = 45^\circ$. Arc $AC$ is made of arcs $AB$ and $BC$, so it measures $2 \times 45 = 90^\circ$.

solve.work: Each arc 360/8 = 45; arc AC through B = 90.

questions.stem: An inscribed angle in a circle measures $20^\circ$ less than the arc it cuts off. What is the measure of the inscribed angle, in degrees?
questions.solution: Let the arc be $a$. The inscribed angle is $\frac{a}{2}$, and it is also $a - 20$. So $\frac{a}{2} = a - 20$, giving $a = 40$ and the angle is $20^\circ$.

questions.stem: Points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie in that order on a circle. Arcs $AB$, $BC$ and $CD$ measure $60^\circ$, $80^\circ$ and $100^\circ$. What is the measure of the inscribed angle $\angle ABC$, in degrees?
questions.solution: Arc $DA = 360 - 60 - 80 - 100 = 120^\circ$. $\angle ABC$ cuts off the arc from $A$ to $C$ that does not contain $B$, which is arc $CD$ plus arc $DA$: $100 + 120 = 220^\circ$. The angle is half of that, $110^\circ$.

solve.work: Angle ABC intercepts arc AC not containing B: 360 - 60 - 80 = 220; angle = 110.

questions.stem: In a circle with center $O$, the minor arc $AB$ measures $110^\circ$. Point $C$ lies on the minor arc $AB$. What is the measure of the inscribed angle $\angle ACB$, in degrees?
